1: This article names the country and fixes its shape. India, that is Bharat, is a Union of States. The States and the Union territories are listed in the First Schedule. The territory of India also takes in any other territories the country may later acquire. A Union of States means one country built out of states under one Constitution.
2: This article gives Parliament the power to admit or establish new States in the Union. Admission or establishment happens by law, on terms and conditions Parliament thinks fit. The article looks short, but it is the door through which new states have entered after 1950.
3: This article lets Parliament change the map of the States by law. It can form a new State by separating or uniting territory. It can increase or diminish the area of any State, alter its boundaries, or change its name. Such a Bill needs the President's recommendation. The concerned State may state its views, but its consent is not required.
4: This article handles what follows a boundary change. A law under article 2 or 3 can also amend the First and Fourth Schedules as needed. It may carry supplemental and consequential provisions, such as changes in representation. Such a law is not counted as an amendment of the Constitution under article 368.
5: This article settled who became a citizen when the Constitution began. A person with domicile in India became a citizen if born in India, or if either parent was born there, or after residing in India for five years before the commencement. It applied once, at the start, on 26 January 1950.
6: This article dealt with people who moved to India from Pakistan around Partition. Such a person was counted a citizen if a parent or grandparent was born in India as the law then defined it. Those who came after 19 July 1948 also needed registration after residence. The article settled citizenship for one migration at one moment in history.
7: This article covered movement the other way. A person who migrated from India to Pakistan after 1 March 1947 was not to be a citizen of India. There was one exception. A person who returned under a permit for resettlement could become a citizen after registration. The article kept citizenship from surviving a permanent move away.
8: This article covered people of Indian origin living abroad. It applied where the person, or a parent or grandparent, was born in India as then defined. The person also had to be living outside India. Such a person could become a citizen by registration. The registration was done by an Indian diplomatic or consular representative.
9: This article is short and firm. A person who voluntarily takes the citizenship of a foreign state cannot be a citizen of India under articles 5, 6, or 8. Citizenship at the commencement could not sit alongside another citizenship of the person's own free choice.
10: This article keeps citizenship going. Anyone who is a citizen under this Part continues to be one, subject to any law Parliament makes. Parliament may later set how citizenship continues or ends. The article bridged the opening rules of the Constitution and the citizenship laws that followed.
11: This article keeps Parliament's power open. Nothing in articles 5 to 10 limits Parliament's right to make laws on citizenship. Parliament may regulate how citizenship is acquired and lost, and all other matters relating to it. This power produced the Citizenship Act, 1955, which governs the subject today.
12: This article defines who counts as the State for this Part. The definition covers the Government and Parliament of India, state governments and legislatures, and local or other bodies under government control or within India. The rights in this Part bind all of these bodies.
13: This article makes fundamental rights stronger than ordinary law. Any law, old or new, that conflicts with these rights stops working to that extent. The word law covers ordinances, rules, orders, and customs. Governments cannot bypass rights by choosing a different legal form.
14: This article says every person is equal before the law and gets equal protection of the laws. The State cannot treat one person better or worse than another in like cases. Courts use it to test arbitrary state action, because unequal treatment without a fair reason usually fails here.
15: This article bans discrimination by the State against citizens only on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. No citizen can be barred from shops, restaurants, hotels, wells, tanks, or public places on those grounds. The State may still make special provisions for women, children, and disadvantaged classes, and for seats in education and jobs.
16: This article promises an equal chance for all citizens to get public jobs. No citizen can be kept out of a government job only for reasons of religion, race, caste, sex, birth, family line, or residence. Parliament or a state legislature may set residence rules for some posts. The State may also reserve posts for backward classes.
17: This article abolishes untouchability. Its practice in any form is forbidden. So is enforcing any disability that arises from it. Parliament backed this with a criminal law against untouchability. No custom, and no payment, can justify treating any person as untouchable.
18: This article stops the State from giving or recognising titles of nobility, and no citizen may accept one from a foreign state. Awards for military or academic distinction are allowed. They cannot be used as titles attached to names. The aim is to keep citizens equal, without ranks the government can hand out.
19: This article gives citizens six freedoms: speech and expression; assembly without arms; forming associations; movement; residence; and any profession or trade. Each freedom can face reasonable limits. The State may set limits for stated public reasons, such as security, public order, or the rights of others. Only citizens hold these freedoms.
20: This article protects people in criminal cases in three ways. A person cannot be punished under a law that was not in force when the act was done. A person cannot be tried and punished twice for the same offence. And a person cannot be forced to testify against himself. These protections apply to everyone, citizen or not.
21: This article says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except by a fair legal procedure. Courts have read it broadly. The right to life means a life with dignity, and it covers things like a clean environment, health, shelter, and privacy. It is the most used fundamental right in Indian courts.
22: This article protects people who are arrested. An arrested person must be told the reason. The person may consult a lawyer of choice. The person must be produced before a magistrate within twenty four hours. Preventive detention is allowed, but only under a fair procedure with advisory boards and time limits set by law.
23: This article bans traffic in human beings and forced labour in any form. No one can be made to work without pay, and bonded labour is illegal. The State may require compulsory service for a public purpose, such as during an emergency. It must not impose that service by religion, caste, or class.
24: This article bans employing children below fourteen in factories, mines, or other risky work. It protects children from labour that harms health and safety. It works with the right to education in Article 21A, so children study instead of doing dangerous work.
25: This article guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise, and spread religion, for all persons. The State may regulate religious activity for public order, morality, and health. It may also open Hindu religious institutions to all classes. Wearing and carrying kirpans counts as part of the Sikh religion.
26: This article lets every religious group manage its own affairs. A group may set up institutions, own property, and run them by its own faith. This holds subject to public order, morality, and health. The State may still pass laws for social reform, or for opening institutions to all classes.
27: This article stops the State from forcing any person to pay taxes whose money is used to promote one religion. Public money collected from all cannot be spent on the institutions of a single faith. This keeps the state out of religious promotion.
28: This article keeps religious teaching out of institutions maintained fully by government funds. Institutions that receive aid may give religious teaching, but only with consent. No student can be made to attend religious teaching or worship without the consent of a guardian.
29: This article protects the culture and language of any section of citizens, including minorities. Any citizen has the right to conserve a distinct language, script, or culture. No citizen can be denied entry to a State run institution only for reasons of religion, race, caste, or language.
30: This article gives religious and language minorities the right to start and run their own schools and colleges. The State cannot be unfair to such institutions when giving aid. Laws that control them must respect the minority's choice of what is taught and who teaches.
31: This article was omitted by the Constitution Forty fourth Amendment Act in 1978. It earlier made the right to property a fundamental right. Property is now only an ordinary legal right under Article 300A. The State may take property for public use with a valid law and a fair process.
32: This article is the right to enforce every other right in this Part. A person whose rights are broken may go straight to the Supreme Court. The Court can pass directions and writs such as habeas corpus and certiorari. This remedy is itself a fundamental right. It cannot be suspended except as the Constitution allows during an emergency.
33: This article lets Parliament limit or end the fundamental rights of members of the armed forces, police, and intelligence services. The limits exist so that they keep discipline and do their duties properly. This is why service rules can curb speech and association rights for those in the forces.
34: This article protects persons acting under martial law from suits for acts done in that role. It also lets Parliament shield officers and servants of the Union for acts done to keep or restore order in areas where martial law holds.
35: This article gives Parliament alone the power to make laws for enforcing the rights in this Part. That includes the power to fix punishment for acts the Constitution declares to be crimes. State legislatures cannot make such laws. This keeps the sanctions for rights uniform across the country.
36: This article defines one word for this Part. The State has the same meaning here as in Part III. It covers the Government and Parliament of India, state governments and legislatures, and local or other authorities under government control. The directive principles therefore guide every arm of the State.
37: This article sets the legal force of the directive principles. Courts cannot enforce them. Yet the principles are fundamental in the governance of the country, and the State must apply them in making laws. They guide; they do not bind like fundamental rights. This balance between ideal and law runs through Part IV.
38: This article asks the State to build a just social order. Justice, social, economic, and political, must inform all the institutions of national life. The State must secure and protect such an order. The State must also strive to reduce inequalities in income. And it must work to remove inequalities in status, facilities, and opportunities. These duties run among individuals and among groups in different areas or lines of work.
39: This article lists goals for State policy. Citizens, men and women equally, should have an adequate means of livelihood. The ownership of material resources should serve the common good. Wealth and means of production should not concentrate in few hands to the common harm. Men and women should get equal pay for equal work. Children should be protected from exploitation, and no one should be forced by need into work unsuited to their age or strength.
40: This article asks the State to organise village panchayats. These bodies should have such powers and authority as they need to work as units of self-government. The aim is democracy at the village level. The 73rd Amendment later gave panchayats constitutional status, regular elections, and a list of local subjects.
41: This article sets social goals for the State to pursue within its economic capacity. The State should make effective provision for the right to work, to education, and to public help in unemployment, old age, sickness, and disablement. It also covers other cases of undeserved want. The promise is real, but it is shaped by what the economy can carry.
42: This article asks the State to secure just and humane conditions of work. It also directs the State to provide maternity relief. Rules on working hours, safety, and maternity benefit in Indian law draw on this principle. The article keeps the dignity of the worker in view.
43: This article asks the State to secure workers a living wage. Workers in farming, industry, or any other line should get work, a living wage, and conditions that allow a decent standard of life. They should also enjoy leisure and social and cultural opportunities. The State should in particular promote cottage industries, on an individual or cooperative basis.
44: This article asks the State to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens across India. A civil code covers matters such as marriage, divorce, inheritance, and adoption. At present these matters run on different personal laws for different communities. One common code would place every citizen under the same civil rules. The article says the State shall endeavour, so it stands as a goal, not a settled law.
45: This article now covers the earliest years of childhood. The State shall endeavour to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years. The original text promised free education up to the age of fourteen. The 86th Amendment moved that promise into Article 21A as a right, and gave this article its present form.
46: This article asks the State to promote, with special care, the educational and economic interests of the weaker sections of the people. It names the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes in particular. The State must protect them from social injustice and all forms of exploitation. Support in education and jobs for these groups draws on this principle.
47: This article makes nutrition, living standards, and public health primary duties of the State. The State must raise the level of nutrition and the standard of living of its people. It must improve public health. The State should also endeavour to stop the consumption of intoxicating drinks and of drugs that injure health, except for medicinal purposes.
48: This article asks the State to organise agriculture and animal husbandry on modern and scientific lines. The State should take steps to preserve and improve the breeds. It should prohibit the slaughter of cows and calves and of other milch and draught cattle. The article joins farm modernisation with the protection of cattle.
49: This article makes the protection of national monuments an obligation of the State. It covers monuments, places, and objects of artistic or historic interest. They must be declared by law to be of national importance. The State must protect each one. It must save them from damage, disfigurement, destruction, removal, disposal, or export.
50: This article asks the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services. The aim is that officers who run the administration should not also decide cases. Separation protects fairness in trials. The criminal procedure reforms of 1973 carried this principle into practice.
51: This article sets out the country's aims abroad. The State shall promote international peace and security. It shall maintain just and honourable relations between nations. It shall foster respect for international law and treaty obligations. And it shall encourage the settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
52: This article creates the office of the President of India. It runs to a single line. The President is the head of the Union. The articles that follow set out how the President is elected, what the office may do, and how a President can leave office.
53: This article vests the executive power of the Union in the President. It is exercised directly or through officers subordinate to the President, in accordance with the Constitution. The supreme command of the defence forces also rests with the President, and law regulates its use. The article does not shift functions that existing law gives to states or other authorities. Parliament may still confer functions on other authorities.
54: This article sets up the election of the President. The President is elected by an electoral college. It consists of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States. For this purpose, State includes the National Capital Territory of Delhi and the Union territory of Puducherry. Nominated members do not vote.
55: This article sets the manner of the presidential election. There shall be uniformity in the scale of representation of the different States, as far as practicable. The value of each member's vote is worked out by formula. This keeps parity between the States as a whole and the Union. The election follows proportional representation by single transferable vote. Voting is by secret ballot.
56: This article fixes the President's term at five years from the date of entering office. The President may resign by writing under hand to the Vice-President. The President may also be removed for violation of the Constitution, through impeachment under article 61. A resignation is communicated by the Vice-President to the Speaker of the House of the People.
57: This article allows re-election. A person who holds, or has held, office as President is eligible for election to that office again. This holds subject to the other provisions of the Constitution. Several Presidents have served more than one term under this rule.
58: This article sets the qualifications for President. A candidate must be a citizen of India. The candidate must have completed thirty five years of age. And the candidate must be qualified for election to the House of the People. A person holding an office of profit under the Government of India, a State, or a controlled authority is not eligible. The President, Vice-President, Governors, and Ministers do not count as holding offices of profit here.
59: This article sets the conditions of the President's office. The President cannot be a member of Parliament or a state legislature. Any such seat falls vacant on election as President. The President cannot hold any other office of profit. The President may use the official residences without rent and draws emoluments set by Parliament. Those emoluments cannot be reduced during the term.
60: This article prescribes the oath for the President. Every President, and every person acting in that office, must make and subscribe an oath or affirmation before entering upon the office. It is made in the presence of the Chief Justice of India. In his absence, the senior-most available Judge of the Supreme Court administers it. The oath binds the President to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution.
61: This article sets the impeachment procedure for the President. The charge is for violation of the Constitution. Either House of Parliament may prefer it. The proposal needs fourteen days' notice in writing signed by at least one fourth of the members of that House. It must pass by a majority of two thirds of the total membership. The other House then investigates the charge. The President may appear and be represented. If that House sustains the charge by the same majority, the President stands removed from office.
62: This article covers the timing of presidential elections. An election for an expiring term must be completed before the term ends. If a vacancy arises by death, resignation, or removal, the election is held as soon as possible. It must happen within six months of the vacancy. A person elected to fill the vacancy is entitled to the full term of five years.
63: This article creates the office of the Vice-President of India. Like article 52, it runs to a single line. The Vice-President is the second highest office of the Union. Article 64 makes the Vice-President the ex officio Chairman of the Council of States.
64: This article makes the Vice-President the ex officio Chairman of the Council of States. The Council of States is the Rajya Sabha. The Vice-President cannot hold any other office of profit. While acting as President, the Vice-President does not perform the duties of Chairman. The same applies while discharging the President’s functions under article 65.
65: This article covers gaps in the presidency. The office may fall vacant by death, resignation, or removal. The Vice-President then acts as President until a new President is elected. The President may also be unable to act owing to absence, illness, or any other cause. The Vice-President then discharges the functions until the President resumes duty. While so acting, the Vice-President has all the powers and immunities of the President.
66: This article covers the election of the Vice-President. The electoral college consists of members of both Houses of Parliament. The election follows proportional representation by single transferable vote, by secret ballot. The Vice-President cannot be a member of Parliament or a state legislature. A candidate must be a citizen of India, at least thirty five years old, and qualified for election to the Council of States. A person holding an office of profit is not eligible.
67: This article fixes the Vice-President's term at five years. The Vice-President may resign by writing to the President. The Vice-President may also be removed by a resolution of the Council of States. The resolution must be agreed to by the House of the People. Notice of at least fourteen days is required, and the resolution must carry a majority of all the then members of the Council.
68: This article covers the timing of Vice-Presidential elections. An election for an expiring term must be completed before the term ends. If a vacancy arises by death, resignation, or removal, the election is held as soon as possible after it occurs. The person elected serves the full term, subject to article 67.
69: This article prescribes the oath for the Vice-President. The oath or affirmation is made before entering office. It is subscribed before the President, or a person appointed by the President for the purpose. The Vice-President swears true faith and allegiance to the Constitution.
70: This article is a safety valve. Parliament may make provision for the discharge of the President's functions in any contingency not covered by this Chapter. It fills gaps the framers could not list. A sudden situation with no President and no Vice-President in place would be handled under a law made here.
71: This article deals with election disputes for the President and the Vice-President. All doubts and disputes from such elections are decided by the Supreme Court, and its decision is final. If an election is declared void, acts done by that person in office stay valid until the date of the decision. Parliament may regulate the related matters by law. A vacancy in the electoral college does not invalidate an election.
72: This article gives the President the power of mercy. The President may grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment. The President may also suspend, remit, or commute a sentence. This covers court martial cases, offences against laws on the Union List, and death sentences. The Governor's power over a death sentence is not affected. This power is the last door of relief in the justice system.
73: This article defines the reach of the Union’s executive power. It extends to matters on which Parliament can make laws. It also covers rights, authority, and jurisdiction from any treaty or agreement. These are exercised by the Government of India. Until Parliament provides otherwise, states may keep exercising functions in matters where Parliament can legislate. The article draws the outer line of Union administration.
74: This article creates the Council of Ministers, with the Prime Minister at its head, to aid and advise the President. The President must act in accordance with that advice. The President may once require the Council to reconsider its advice. The advice after reconsideration binds the President. Courts cannot inquire into what advice the Ministers tendered. The real executive thus sits in the Council, not the formal head.
75: This article covers the appointment and responsibility of Ministers. The President appoints the Prime Minister. Other Ministers are appointed on the Prime Minister's advice. The Council of Ministers cannot exceed fifteen per cent of the membership of the House of the People. A member disqualified for defection cannot be a Minister during that disqualification. Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President. The Council is collectively responsible to the House of the People. The President administers to each Minister the oaths of office and secrecy.
76: This article creates the Attorney-General for India. The President appoints a person qualified to be a Judge of the Supreme Court. The Attorney-General advises the Government of India on legal matters referred by the President. The office also carries duties of a legal character. The Attorney-General has the right of audience in all courts in India. The office is held during the pleasure of the President.
77: This article sets how the Government of India transacts its business. All executive action is taken in the name of the President. Orders and instruments in the President's name are authenticated under rules. Properly authenticated orders cannot be questioned merely because they were not made by the President. The President makes rules for the convenient transaction of business and allocates business among Ministers. These are the Business Rules of the Government.
78: This article lists the Prime Minister's duties toward the President. The Prime Minister must communicate all decisions of the Council of Ministers on administration and on proposals for legislation. The Prime Minister must furnish information on administration that the President calls for. And any matter decided by a Minister alone must go before the Council if the President so requires. This keeps the head of State informed.
79: This article creates the Parliament of the Union. It consists of the President and two Houses known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People. The Council of States is the Rajya Sabha. The House of the People is the Lok Sabha. The President is part of Parliament though not a member of either House.
80: This article fixes the composition of the Council of States. It has not more than two hundred and thirty eight representatives of the States and the Union territories. The President also nominates twelve members with special knowledge of literature, science, art, or social service. The allocation of state seats follows the Fourth Schedule. State representatives are elected by the elected members of the state assembly by proportional representation.
81: This article fixes the composition of the House of the People. It has not more than five hundred and thirty members chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the States. It may also have not more than twenty members from the Union territories. Seats are allotted to the States so that the ratio of seats to population stays the same for all, so far as practicable. Population means the figures of the last published census.
82: This article provides for readjustment after each census. The allocation of seats in the House of the People and the division of States into constituencies are readjusted by law. Parliament decides the authority and the manner. By amendment, the present allocation stands frozen at the 1971 census figures until the first census after 2026 is published.
83: This article fixes the duration of the two Houses. The Council of States is not subject to dissolution. About one third of its members retire every second year. The House of the People continues for five years unless sooner dissolved. While a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, Parliament may extend the term by law, a year at a time. The extension cannot run more than six months past the emergency.
84: This article sets the qualifications for membership of Parliament. A person must be a citizen of India and must make and subscribe the oath in the Third Schedule. For the Council of States the minimum age is thirty years. For the House of the People it is twenty five years. Parliament may add further qualifications by law.
85: This article covers sessions of Parliament. The President summons each House from time to time. Six months shall not pass between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next. This rule keeps Parliament meeting regularly. The President may prorogue the Houses and may dissolve the House of the People.
86: This article gives the President a right of direct communication with Parliament. The President may address either House or both Houses together. For that purpose the President may require the attendance of members. The President may also send messages to either House, for example on a pending Bill. The House must consider such a message with all convenient despatch.
87: This article provides for the special address. The President addresses both Houses assembled together at two moments. One is the first session after each general election to the House of the People. The other is the first session of each year. The address informs Parliament of the causes of its summons. Rules of procedure allot time for discussing it.
88: This article opens the Houses to Ministers and the Attorney-General. Each may speak and take part in the proceedings of either House. The right covers joint sittings and committees as well. A Minister who is not a member of a House does not vote there. This lets Ministers pilot business in both Houses.
89: This article provides the officers of the Council of States. The Vice-President of India is the ex officio Chairman. The Council chooses one of its members as Deputy Chairman. It does so as soon as may be after a vacancy arises. The office is refilled each time it falls vacant.
90: This article covers the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States. The Deputy Chairman vacates office on ceasing to be a member of the Council. The Deputy Chairman may resign by writing to the Chairman. Removal is by resolution of the Council. It needs fourteen days' notice and a majority of all the then members.
91: This article covers the Chairman's absence. When the office of Chairman is vacant, the Deputy Chairman performs the duties. If that office is also vacant, a member appointed by the President performs them. During the Chairman's absence at a sitting, the Deputy Chairman presides. If both are absent, the rules of procedure name a person, or the Council chooses one.
92: This article keeps the removal process fair. When a resolution for removing the Chairman is under consideration, the Chairman does not preside. The same rule applies to the Deputy Chairman. The Chairman may speak and otherwise take part in the proceedings while such a resolution is under consideration. Presiding passes to another member for that sitting.
93: This article provides the officers of the House of the People. The House chooses two of its members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker. It does so as soon as may be. Whenever either office falls vacant, the House chooses another member for it.
94: This article covers the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People. Each vacates office on ceasing to be a member of the House. The Speaker resigns by writing to the Deputy Speaker. The Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker. Either may be removed by a resolution of the House after fourteen days' notice, carried by a majority of all the then members.
95: This article covers the Speaker's absence. When the office of Speaker is vacant, the Deputy Speaker performs the duties. If both offices are vacant, a member appointed by the President performs them. During the Speaker's absence at a sitting, the Deputy Speaker presides. If both are absent, the rules of procedure provide, failing which the House chooses a person.
96: This article keeps the Speaker's removal process fair. While a resolution for removing the Speaker is under consideration, the Speaker does not preside. The same rule applies to the Deputy Speaker. The Speaker may speak and take part in the proceedings. In such proceedings the Speaker votes only in the case of an equality of votes.
97: This article provides salaries for the presiding officers. The Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of the Council of States and the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of the House of the People receive salaries and allowances. These are fixed by Parliament by law. Until Parliament makes such a law, they are paid as fixed by rules.
98: This article gives each House its own secretariat. Each House of Parliament has a separate secretarial staff. Posts common to both Houses may still be created. Parliament may by law regulate recruitment and conditions of service. Until then, the President makes rules after consulting the Speaker or the Chairman.
99: This article prescribes the oath for members. Every member of either House must make and subscribe an oath or affirmation before taking a seat. It is made before the President, or a person appointed by him for the purpose. The form is set out in the Third Schedule.
100: This article sets the voting rules of the Houses. Questions at any sitting are decided by a majority of the members present and voting. The Chairman or Speaker does not vote, except at an equality of votes. A House may act despite vacancies in its membership. The quorum is one tenth of the total members. Without a quorum, the Chair adjourns or suspends the meeting.
101: This article governs vacation of seats. No person may be a member of both Houses of Parliament. No person may be a member of Parliament and of a state legislature at once. A seat also falls vacant on disqualification, on resignation in writing to the Chair, and on absence without leave for sixty days. Periods when the House is prorogued do not count toward the sixty days.
102: This article lists the disqualifications for membership. A person is disqualified who holds an office of profit under the Government of India or a State, unless Parliament declares the office exempt. Ministers are not treated as holding offices of profit here. A person of unsound mind declared by a court, an undischarged insolvent, or a voluntary citizen of another country is disqualified. Parliament may add grounds by law. The Tenth Schedule adds disqualification for defection.
103: This article settles doubts about a member’s seat. A question whether a member has become disqualified under article 102 goes to the President. The President decides the question. Before deciding, the President must obtain the opinion of the Election Commission. The President then acts according to that opinion.
104: This article penalises unqualified sitting. A person who sits or votes as a member before taking the oath under article 99 is liable to a penalty. The same applies to a person who knows he is not qualified, or is disqualified, or is prohibited from sitting. The penalty is five hundred rupees for each day of such sitting or voting.
105: This article protects speech in Parliament. There is freedom of speech in Parliament, subject to the Constitution and the rules of procedure. No member is liable in any court for anything said or any vote given in Parliament or its committees. Publication under the authority of a House enjoys the same protection. Other powers and privileges are defined by Parliament by law. Until so defined, they remain those the House held at the commencement of the Constitution.
106: This article provides pay for members. Members of either House receive salaries and allowances. These are determined by Parliament by law. Until such a law is made, they are paid under rules made by the President. The provision keeps member pay in the hands of Parliament itself.
107: This article covers how Bills pass. A Bill may originate in either House, subject to the special rules for Money Bills. A Bill is not passed unless both Houses agree to it. A pending Bill does not lapse on prorogation. On dissolution of the House of the People, a Bill pending there lapses, and so does a Bill passed by it and pending in the Council. A Bill pending in the Council that the House of the People has not passed does not lapse.
108: This article resolves deadlocks between the Houses. A joint sitting may be called if the other House rejects a Bill. It may also be called on final disagreement over amendments, or after six months of delay. The President notifies the intention and summons both Houses together. The Bill then passes by a majority of the members present and voting. Money Bills and constitutional amendment Bills are outside this route.
109: This article gives the House of the People sole control over Money Bills. A Money Bill cannot be introduced in the Council of States. After the House of the People passes one, the Council has fourteen days. The Council returns it with recommendations. The House of the People may accept or reject them. If the Council does not return the Bill in fourteen days, it is deemed passed by both Houses.
110: This article defines a Money Bill. A Bill is a Money Bill if it deals only with taxes, borrowing, or the custody of the Consolidated Fund. It also covers charged expenditure, and the receipt and audit of accounts. Fines and licence fees do not make a Bill a Money Bill. If a question arises, the Speaker's decision is final. Every Money Bill carries the Speaker's certificate.
111: This article covers the President's assent. When both Houses pass a Bill, it is presented to the President. The President declares assent or withholds it. The President may return a Bill, other than a Money Bill, once for reconsideration. If Parliament passes it again, with or without changes, the President must assent. For a Money Bill the return option is not available.
112: This article creates the Union Budget in constitutional terms. The President causes an annual financial statement to be laid before both Houses. It shows the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for the year. Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India is shown separately from other expenditure. The statement is what people commonly call the Budget.
113: This article separates the two kinds of spending. Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India is discussed but not voted on. It covers salaries of offices fixed by the Constitution itself. All other expenditure goes to the House of the People as demands for grants. The House may assent to a demand or refuse it. No demand can be made except on the President's recommendation.
114: This article turns grants into law. After the House of the People makes grants under article 113, an Appropriation Bill is introduced. It authorises withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund of India for the grants. Amendments cannot vary the amount or the destination of any grant. Subject to articles 115 and 116, no money leaves the Fund except under an appropriation made by law.
115: This article covers shortfalls. If the money granted for a service proves insufficient, a supplementary grant is made. Additional grants may be needed for a new service. Spending in excess of a grant is regularised in the same way. The procedure of articles 112, 113, and 114 applies to these statements and demands as well.
116: This article covers advance spending. The House of the People may make a grant in advance for part of a year while the full Budget waits. This is the vote on account. Votes of credit and exceptional grants cover other urgent needs. The rules of articles 113 and 114 apply to all of them.
117: This article gives financial Bills special handling. Some Bills need the President’s recommendation to be introduced. These are Bills and amendments dealing with the matters of article 110. A Bill imposing such charges cannot be introduced in the Council of States. Any Bill involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund also needs the President’s recommendation before a House passes it.
118: This article lets each House make its own rules. Each House may regulate its procedure and the conduct of its business, subject to the Constitution. Until rules are made, the rules of the Dominion Legislature continue. The President, after consulting the Chairman and the Speaker, makes rules for joint sittings. At a joint sitting the Speaker presides.
119: This article lets Parliament set deadlines for money matters. Parliament may by law regulate the procedure and the conduct of business in each House. This applies to financial matters and to Bills for appropriation from the Consolidated Fund. The purpose is the timely completion of financial business.
120: This article sets the language of Parliament. Business is transacted in Hindi or in English. A member who cannot adequately express himself in either may speak in his mother tongue with the permission of the Chair. The Constitution allowed English to drop away after fifteen years. Parliament has by law continued its use.
121: This article limits debate about judges. No discussion shall take place in Parliament on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge in the discharge of his duties. There is one opening. A motion for an address to the President for the removal of the judge may be discussed.
122: This article shields Parliament’s work from the courts. No court can question a proceeding of Parliament for a claimed irregularity of procedure. The same shield covers the officers who regulate procedure or keep order. Such complaints belong inside Parliament. Courts step aside here.
123: This article lets the President make law when Parliament is not in session. If circumstances call for immediate action, the President may promulgate an Ordinance. It has the same force as an Act of Parliament. It must be laid before both Houses. It ceases to operate six weeks after Parliament reassembles. Any provision Parliament could not enact is void.
124: This article establishes the Supreme Court of India. It consists of the Chief Justice of India and other Judges. The text sets a ceiling of seven other Judges until Parliament prescribes more, and Parliament has prescribed more. Judges are appointed by the President. The text, as amended by the 99th Amendment, vests the recommendation in the National Judicial Appointments Commission. The Supreme Court struck that Commission down in 2015, and appointments continue under the collegium practice.
125: This article provides for judges' pay. Judges of the Supreme Court receive salaries determined by Parliament by law. Until a law is made, the Second Schedule fixes them. Judges also receive privileges, allowances, and pension rights as determined by or under law made by Parliament.
126: This article covers an empty Chief Justice's chair. When the office of Chief Justice of India is vacant, the duties are performed by another Judge of the Court. The same applies when the Chief Justice is absent or otherwise unable to act. The President appoints the Judge for the purpose. The arrangement keeps the Court always under a head.
127: This article covers a shortage of judges. If there is no quorum of Judges to hold a session of the Supreme Court, a High Court Judge may sit as an ad hoc Judge. The text routes the request through the judicial appointments body on a reference by the Chief Justice. The designated Judge attends the sittings as a priority duty.
128: This article lets retired judges return to the bench. A person who has held office as a Supreme Court or High Court Judge may sit and act as a Judge of the Supreme Court. The request is made with the previous consent of the President. While sitting, the person has all the jurisdiction, powers, and privileges of a Judge of the Court.
129: This article makes the Supreme Court a court of record. A court of record keeps a permanent account of its proceedings, and that account carries full legal weight. The Supreme Court has all the powers of such a court. These include the power to punish for contempt of itself.
130: This article fixes the seat of the Supreme Court. The Court sits in Delhi, and the Chief Justice of India may appoint other places for it to sit with the approval of the President. This allows the Court to hold sittings outside Delhi when needed.
131: This article gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in federal disputes. It hears, to the exclusion of other courts, disputes between the Government of India and one or more States. It also hears disputes between States. Disputes involving Union territories on one side are included. Matters assigned by law to other forums, such as inter state river water disputes, stand outside.
132: This article opens appeals on constitutional questions. An appeal lies to the Supreme Court from a judgment, decree, or final order of a High Court. The High Court must certify under article 134A that the case involves a substantial question of law about the interpretation of the Constitution. Any party may then appeal on the ground that the question was wrongly decided.
133: This article opens civil appeals. An appeal lies to the Supreme Court from a judgment of a High Court in a civil proceeding. The High Court must certify under article 134A. The grounds are a substantial question of law of general importance, or that the case otherwise needs the Supreme Court's decision. Appeals from a single Judge of a High Court lie only if Parliament provides.
134: This article opens criminal appeals. An appeal lies to the Supreme Court from a High Court decision in a criminal proceeding. One ground is that the High Court reversed an acquittal and sentenced the accused to death. Certified cases form another ground. Parliament may by law add further criminal appeal powers.
135: This article carries the Federal Court's powers forward. Until Parliament provides otherwise, the Supreme Court holds the jurisdiction and powers of the Federal Court under existing law. This covers matters not dealt with by articles 133 and 134. It preserved continuity when the Supreme Court replaced the Federal Court in 1950.
136: This article gives the Supreme Court a wide discretionary power. It may grant special leave to appeal from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal in India. The grant is entirely at the Court's discretion. Orders of courts and tribunals under armed forces law are excluded.
137: This article allows the Supreme Court to revisit its own decisions. The Court may review any judgment or order it has passed. The power is subject to any law made by Parliament and to the Court's rules under article 145. Review is exceptional, not a routine second appeal.
138: This article allows the Supreme Court's jurisdiction to grow. Parliament may by law confer further jurisdiction and powers over matters in the Union List. The Government of India and a State may also agree to confer jurisdiction on the Court. Such an agreement takes effect only if Parliament provides for it by law.
139: This article lets Parliament expand the Supreme Court's writ powers. Parliament may by law confer power to issue directions, orders, or writs. The writs include habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari. This can serve purposes beyond the fundamental rights jurisdiction of article 32.
140: This article lets Parliament add supporting powers to the Supreme Court. Parliament may by law confer supplemental powers on the Court. They must not be inconsistent with the Constitution. The purpose is to enable the Court to discharge its functions more effectively.
141: This article makes Supreme Court precedent binding. The law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts within the territory of India. Lower courts must follow what the Supreme Court has laid down. Only the Court itself can revisit its own precedent, under the review power of article 137.
142: This article gives the Supreme Court the tools to finish the job. In exercising its jurisdiction, the Court may pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice in a matter before it. Such decrees operate across the whole of India. The Court also has powers to secure attendance, production of documents, and discovery, subject to Parliament's law.
143: This article lets the President consult the Supreme Court. The President may refer a question of law or fact of public importance for the Court's opinion. The Court reports its opinion after hearing as it thinks fit. The President may also refer a dispute of the kind excluded from article 131. The opinions are advisory, but they carry great weight.
144: This article commands support for the Supreme Court. All authorities, civil and judicial, in the territory of India shall act in aid of the Supreme Court. Administrations and courts alike must help the Court enforce its process and orders. The duty is general and continuous.
145: This article lets the Supreme Court make its own rules. The Court may, with the approval of the President, regulate its practice and procedure. Rules may fix the minimum number of Judges for any purpose. They provide for the powers of single Judges and Division Courts. Constitutional questions and references under article 143 need at least five Judges.
146: This article covers the Supreme Court's staff and costs. Appointments of officers and servants are made by the Chief Justice or a Judge or officer directed by him. Conditions of service are set by rules of the Chief Justice, subject to Parliament's law. The administrative expenses of the Court are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
147: This article is a reading rule. It applies to this Chapter and to Chapter V of Part VI. References to a substantial question of law about the Constitution include questions about the Government of India Act, 1935, and orders made under it. It lets the old law be read smoothly into the new.
148: This article creates the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India. The President appoints the CAG by warrant. Removal is only as for a Supreme Court Judge, on an address of Parliament. The CAG takes an oath before entering office. Salary and conditions are set by Parliament and cannot be varied to the CAG's disadvantage after appointment. The CAG cannot hold further government office after retiring.
149: This article sets the CAG's duties. The Comptroller and Auditor-General performs duties and exercises powers over the accounts of the Union and of the States. Other authorities and bodies can also be brought in by law. The office audits the public spending of the country at both levels.
150: This article fixes the form of public accounts. The accounts of the Union and of the States are kept in the form the President prescribes. The President acts on the advice of the Comptroller and Auditor-General. This keeps the forms consistent across the country.
151: This article routes audit reports. Reports on the accounts of the Union go to the President, who lays them before each House of Parliament. Reports on the accounts of a State go to the Governor, who lays them before the state legislature. These reports feed the Public Accounts Committees.
152: This article defines the word State for Part VI. It excludes the State of Jammu and Kashmir, reflecting that State's old special position. Since 2019 the territory is a Union territory with a legislature. The printed text of the article still carries the old carve out.
153: This article provides a Governor for each State. The Governor is the constitutional head, like the President at the Union. The same person may serve as Governor of two or more States. This has been done in practice from time to time.
154: This article vests the executive power of a State in the Governor. It is exercised directly or through officers subordinate to the Governor, in accordance with the Constitution. The article does not transfer functions that existing law gives to other authorities. Parliament or the state legislature may still confer functions elsewhere by law.
155: This article covers the appointment of a Governor. The Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal. Governors are not elected by the people of the State. The Union appoints the head of each State. The office is thus a constitutional appointment made at the Centre.
156: This article fixes the Governor's term. The Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President. The Governor may resign by writing addressed to the President. Subject to that, the term is five years from entering office. A Governor continues until a successor takes charge.
157: This article sets the qualifications for Governor. The person must be a citizen of India. The person must have completed thirty five years of age. These are the only conditions the Constitution states for the office. Parliament has not added more by law.
158: This article sets the conditions of the Governor's office. The Governor cannot be a member of Parliament or of a state legislature. The Governor cannot hold any other office of profit. The Governor may use the official residences without rent. Emoluments and allowances are set by Parliament. Where one person is Governor of two or more States, the emoluments are shared as the President orders.
159: This article prescribes the Governor's oath. Every Governor makes and subscribes an oath or affirmation before entering office. It is made in the presence of the Chief Justice of the relevant High Court. In his absence, the senior-most Judge of that Court administers it. The oath is to preserve, protect, and defend the Constitution.
160: This article is a safety valve for the states. The President may make provision for the discharge of the Governor's functions in any contingency this Chapter does not cover. It fills gaps, much as article 70 does for the President.
161: This article gives the Governor the power of mercy in state matters. The Governor may grant pardons, reprieves, respites, or remissions of punishment. The Governor may suspend, remit, or commute a sentence. This covers offences against laws on which the state legislature can make laws. The Governor's power runs beside the President's under article 72.
162: This article defines the reach of a State's executive power. It extends to matters on which the state legislature can make laws. In matters where both the State and the Union can legislate, the State's power is subject to the Union's. The article draws the outer line of state administration.
163: This article creates the state Council of Ministers. There shall be a Council of Ministers with the Chief Minister at the head, to aid and advise the Governor. The Governor acts on advice, except where the Constitution requires the Governor to act in discretion. Whether a matter is discretionary is decided by the Governor, and that decision is final. Courts cannot inquire into the advice tendered.
164: This article covers state Ministers. The Governor appoints the Chief Minister. Other Ministers are appointed on the Chief Minister’s advice. A state Council cannot exceed fifteen per cent of the Assembly’s strength, and the minimum is twelve. A member disqualified for defection cannot be a Minister during that time. Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Governor. The Council is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
165: This article creates the Advocate-General for the State. The Governor appoints a person qualified to be a High Court Judge. The Advocate-General advises the State Government on legal matters referred by the Governor. The office carries duties of a legal character. It is held during the pleasure of the Governor, with remuneration the Governor determines. Article 177 gives the office a voice in the state legislature.
166: This article sets how a State Government transacts business. All executive action is taken in the name of the Governor. Orders in his name are authenticated under rules. An authenticated order cannot be questioned for not being made by the Governor personally. The Governor also makes rules for the transaction of business. He allocates that business among Ministers.
167: This article lists the Chief Minister’s duties toward the Governor. The Chief Minister must pass on to the Governor all decisions of the Council on administration and on Bills. He must also give the Governor information on administration that is asked for. And a matter decided by a Minister alone must go before the Council if the Governor so requires.
168: This article creates a Legislature for every State. It consists of the Governor and one or two Houses. Where there are two Houses, one is the Legislative Council and the other is the Legislative Assembly. Where there is only one House, it is the Legislative Assembly. Only some States have a Legislative Council. Most States are unicameral, with only the Assembly.
169: This article lets a State change its own shape of legislature. Parliament may by law abolish the Legislative Council of a State that has one. It may also create a Council in a State that has none. The State's Assembly must first pass a resolution by a special majority. Such a law is not treated as an amendment of the Constitution under article 368.
170: This article fixes the size of the Legislative Assembly. Each Assembly has not more than five hundred and not less than sixty members. They are chosen by direct election from territorial constituencies in the State. Constituencies are drawn so that the ratio of seats to population stays the same, so far as practicable. Population means the last published census figures.
171: This article fixes the composition of the Legislative Council. A Council cannot exceed one third of the Assembly's strength, with a minimum of forty members. One third are elected by local bodies such as municipalities and district boards. Another one third are elected by members of the Assembly. One twelfth each come from graduates and teachers. The Governor nominates the remaining one sixth from fields like literature, science, art, and social service.
172: This article fixes the duration of State Legislatures. Every Legislative Assembly continues for five years unless sooner dissolved. The Legislative Council is not subject to dissolution. About one third of its members retire every second year. While a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, Parliament may extend an Assembly's term by law, a year at a time.
173: This article sets the qualifications for membership of a State Legislature. A person must be a citizen of India and must make and subscribe the prescribed oath. For the Legislative Assembly the minimum age is twenty five years. For the Legislative Council it is thirty years. The law may add further qualifications.
174: This article covers sessions of the State Legislature. The Governor summons the House or each House from time to time. Six months shall not pass between the last sitting of one session and the first sitting of the next. This keeps every State Legislature meeting regularly. The Governor may prorogue the House or either House. The Governor may also dissolve the Legislative Assembly.
175: This article gives the Governor a right of direct communication with the legislature. The Governor may address the Legislative Assembly, or either House, or both Houses together. For that purpose the Governor may require the attendance of members. The Governor may also send messages to the House or Houses, for example on a pending Bill. A House must consider such a message with all convenient despatch.
176: This article provides for the special address by the Governor. The Governor addresses the legislature at two moments. One is the first session after each general election to the Legislative Assembly. The other is the first session of each year. The address informs the legislature of the causes of its summons. Rules of procedure allot time for discussing it.
177: This article opens the Houses to Ministers and the Advocate-General. Each may speak and take part in the proceedings of the Legislative Assembly, or of either House where the State has a Council. The right covers joint sittings and committees as well. A Minister who is not a member of a House does not vote there. This lets Ministers pilot business across the legislature.
178: This article provides the officers of the Legislative Assembly. The Assembly chooses two of its members as Speaker and Deputy Speaker. It does so as soon as may be. Whenever either office falls vacant, the Assembly chooses another member for it.
179: This article covers the Speaker and the Deputy Speaker of an Assembly. Each vacates office on ceasing to be a member of the Assembly. The Speaker resigns by writing to the Deputy Speaker. The Deputy Speaker resigns to the Speaker. Either may be removed by a resolution of the Assembly after fourteen days' notice, carried by a majority of all the then members.
180: This article covers the Speaker's absence. When the office of Speaker is vacant, the Deputy Speaker performs the duties. If both offices are vacant, a member appointed by the Governor performs them. During the Speaker's absence at a sitting, the Deputy Speaker presides. If both are absent, the rules of procedure provide, failing which the Assembly chooses a person.
181: This article keeps the Speaker's removal process fair. While a resolution for removing the Speaker is under consideration, the Speaker does not preside. The same rule applies to the Deputy Speaker. The Speaker may speak and take part in the proceedings. In such proceedings the Speaker votes only in the case of an equality of votes.
182: This article provides the officers of the Legislative Council. The Council of every State having one chooses two of its members as Chairman and Deputy Chairman. It does so as soon as may be. Whenever either office falls vacant, the Council chooses another member for it.
183: This article covers the Chairman and the Deputy Chairman of a Legislative Council. Each vacates office on ceasing to be a member of the Council. The Chairman resigns by writing to the Deputy Chairman. The Deputy Chairman resigns to the Chairman. Either may be removed by a resolution of the Council after fourteen days' notice, carried by a majority of all the then members.
184: This article covers the Chairman's absence. When the office of Chairman is vacant, the Deputy Chairman performs the duties. If that office is also vacant, a member appointed by the Governor performs them. During the Chairman's absence at a sitting, the Deputy Chairman presides. If both are absent, the rules of procedure provide, failing which the Council chooses a person.
185: This article keeps the Chairman's removal process fair. While a resolution for removing the Chairman is under consideration, the Chairman does not preside. The same rule applies to the Deputy Chairman. The Chairman may speak and otherwise take part in the proceedings. Presiding passes to another member for that sitting.
186: This article provides salaries for the presiding officers of State Legislatures. The Speaker and Deputy Speaker of the Assembly, and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Council, receive salaries and allowances. These are fixed by the Legislature of the State by law. Until such a law is made, they are paid as fixed by rules.
187: This article gives each House its own secretariat. The House or each House of a State Legislature has a separate secretarial staff. Common posts may still be created where a State has two Houses. The State Legislature may by law regulate recruitment and conditions of service. Until then, the Governor makes rules after consulting the Speaker or the Chairman.
188: This article prescribes the oath for members of State Legislatures. Every member must make and subscribe an oath or affirmation before taking a seat. It is made before the Governor, or a person appointed by him for the purpose. The form is set out in the Third Schedule.
189: This article sets the voting rules of State Houses. Questions at any sitting are decided by a majority of the members present and voting. The Speaker or Chairman does not vote, except at an equality of votes. A House may act despite vacancies in its membership. The quorum is ten members or one tenth of the House, whichever is greater. Without a quorum, the Chair adjourns or suspends the meeting.
190: This article governs vacation of seats in State Legislatures. No person may be a member of both Houses of the same State's legislature. No person may sit in the legislatures of two or more States at once. A seat also falls vacant on disqualification, on resignation in writing to the Chair, and on absence without leave for sixty days. Periods when the House is prorogued do not count toward the sixty days.
191: This article lists the disqualifications for membership of a State Legislature. A person is disqualified who holds an office of profit under the Government of India or of a State, unless the law declares the office exempt. Ministers are not treated as holding offices of profit here. A person of unsound mind declared by a court, an undischarged insolvent, or a voluntary citizen of another country is disqualified. Parliament may add grounds by law. The Tenth Schedule adds disqualification for defection.
192: This article settles doubts about a State member’s seat. A question whether a member has become disqualified under article 191 goes to the Governor. The Governor decides the question. Before deciding, the Governor must obtain the opinion of the Election Commission. The Governor then acts according to that opinion.
193: This article penalises unqualified sitting in a State Legislature. A person who sits or votes as a member before taking the oath under article 188 is liable to a penalty. The same applies to a person who knows he is not qualified, or is disqualified. The penalty is five hundred rupees for each day of such sitting or voting.
194: This article protects speech in State Legislatures. There is freedom of speech in the Legislature of every State, subject to the Constitution and the rules of procedure. No member is liable in any court for anything said or any vote given in the Legislature or its committees. Publication under the authority of a House enjoys the same protection. Other powers and privileges are as defined by the State Legislature by law.
195: This article provides pay for members of State Legislatures. Members of the Assembly and of the Council receive salaries and allowances. These are determined by the Legislature of the State by law. Until such a law is made, they are paid under rules made by the Governor.
196: This article covers how Bills pass in a State Legislature. A Bill may originate in either House where a State has a Council. A Bill is not passed unless both Houses agree to it. A pending Bill does not lapse on prorogation. On dissolution of the Assembly, a Bill pending there lapses, and so does a Bill passed by it and pending in the Council. A Bill pending in the Council that the Assembly has not passed does not lapse.
197: This article restrains the Legislative Council. If the Council rejects an Assembly Bill, or delays it for three months, the Assembly may pass it again. If the Council then rejects it again, or delays a month, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses. The Assembly can therefore override the Council by patience. Joint sittings, used at the Union, do not exist in the States. Money Bills are outside this article.
198: This article gives the Assembly sole control over State Money Bills. A Money Bill cannot be introduced in the Legislative Council. After the Assembly passes one, the Council has fourteen days. The Council returns it with recommendations. The Assembly may accept or reject them. If the Council does not return the Bill in fourteen days, it is deemed passed by both Houses.
199: This article defines a State Money Bill. A Bill is a Money Bill if it deals only with taxes, borrowing, or the custody of the Consolidated Fund of the State. It also covers charged expenditure, and the receipt and audit of accounts. Fines and licence fees do not make a Bill a Money Bill. If a question arises, the Speaker of the Assembly decides it finally.
200: This article covers the Governor's assent. When the Houses pass a Bill, it is presented to the Governor. The Governor may assent, or withhold assent, or return the Bill for reconsideration. If the legislature passes it again, the Governor must assent. The Governor may also reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President. Reservation is used for Bills that affect larger questions.
201: This article covers reserved Bills. When a Governor reserves a Bill, the President declares assent or withholds it. The President may also direct the Governor to return the Bill to the legislature for reconsideration. If the legislature passes it again, it goes back to the President. Reserved Bills are the Union's window into State legislation.
202: This article creates the State Budget in constitutional terms. The Governor causes an annual financial statement to be laid before the legislature. It shows the estimated receipts and expenditure of the State for the year. Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State is shown separately. The statement is the State's own Budget.
203: This article separates the two kinds of State spending. Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund is discussed but not voted on. All other expenditure goes to the Assembly as demands for grants. The Assembly may assent to a demand or refuse it. No demand can be made except on the Governor's recommendation.
204: This article turns State grants into law. After the Assembly makes grants under article 203, an Appropriation Bill is introduced. It authorises withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund of the State. Amendments cannot vary the amount or the destination of any grant. Subject to articles 205 and 206, no money leaves the Fund except under an appropriation made by law.
205: This article covers State shortfalls. If the money granted for a service proves insufficient, a supplementary grant is made. Additional grants may be needed for a new service. Spending in excess of a grant is regularised the same way. The procedure of articles 202, 203, and 204 applies to these statements and demands as well.
206: This article covers advance spending by a State. The Assembly may make a grant in advance for part of a year while the full Budget waits. This is the vote on account. Votes of credit and exceptional grants cover other urgent needs. The rules of articles 203 and 204 apply to all of them.
207: This article gives State financial Bills special handling. Some Bills need the Governor’s recommendation to be introduced. These are Bills and amendments dealing with the matters of article 199. A Bill imposing such charges cannot be introduced in the Council. Any Bill involving expenditure from the Consolidated Fund of the State also needs the Governor’s recommendation before a House passes it.
208: This article lets each House of a State Legislature make its own rules. A House may regulate its procedure and the conduct of its business, subject to the Constitution. Until rules are made, the rules of the old provincial legislature continue. Where a State has a Council, the Governor, after consulting the Speaker and the Chairman, makes rules for communications between the Houses.
209: This article lets a State set deadlines for its money matters. The Legislature of a State may by law regulate the procedure and conduct of business in its House or Houses. This applies to financial matters and to appropriation Bills. The purpose is the timely completion of financial business.
210: This article sets the language of a State Legislature. Business is transacted in the official language or languages of the State, or in Hindi or in English. A member who cannot adequately express himself may speak in his mother tongue with the Chair's permission. English was to drop away after fifteen years, but the Legislature may by law continue its use.
211: This article limits debate about judges in State Legislatures. No discussion shall take place on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge in the discharge of his duties. There is one opening. A motion for an address to the President for the removal of the judge may be discussed.
212: This article shields State Legislature proceedings from the courts. No court can question a proceeding of the Legislature for a claimed irregularity of procedure. The presiding officers who regulate procedure or keep order are also outside the courts' reach. Procedural complaints belong inside the Legislature. Courts step aside here.
213: This article lets the Governor make law when the State Legislature is not in session. If circumstances call for immediate action, the Governor may promulgate an Ordinance. It has the same force as an Act of the Legislature. It must be laid before the legislature. It ceases to operate six weeks after the legislature reassembles. A provision the legislature could not enact is void.
226: This article gives every High Court wide power to issue directions, orders, or writs. The writs include habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari. A High Court can issue them for fundamental rights and also for other legal rights, which makes this power wider than Article 32. The writ can reach any person or government within the court's territories. An interim order made without notice to the other side can be vacated on application.
238: This article is omitted. The official edition prints no entry for it. The table of contents lists it as omitted, under Part VII, which the Constitution itself prints as omitted. The article belonged to the old scheme for States in Part B of the First Schedule.
239: This article governs the running of Union territories. Each one is run by the President through an administrator he appoints. The administrator acts as much or as little as the President directs. The President may give the job to the Governor of a nearby State. Parliament may change the whole arrangement by law.
240: This article gives the President a direct lawmaking power for small Union territories. The President may make regulations for the peace, progress, and good government of the islands and other small territories named in it. These cover the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Lakshadweep, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Ladakh. A regulation may repeal or amend a Parliament Act applying to the territory. When made, it has the force of an Act of Parliament.
241: This article covers High Courts for Union territories. Parliament may by law constitute a High Court for a Union territory. It may also declare an existing court there to be a High Court. The law may extend or restrict the jurisdiction of such a court. Delhi has its own High Court under this article. Other territories are covered by neighbouring High Courts.
242: This article no longer exists. It had provided for the old State of Coorg. That State was abolished on the reorganisation of 1956. The 7th Amendment omitted the article in that year. The territory became a district of Mysore, which is now Karnataka.
243: This article defines the words of Part IX. A district means a district of a State. A Gram Sabha is the body of registered voters in a village area. A Panchayat is an institution of self-government for a rural area, at the village, intermediate, or district level. A Intermediate level means a level between village and district. These definitions anchor the panchayat provisions that follow.
244: This article links the schedules to the administration of special areas. The Fifth Schedule applies to the Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in States other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, and Mizoram. The Sixth Schedule applies to the tribal areas of those four States. The schedules create special governance arrangements for these areas. Each schedule has its own mechanism of councils and Governor's powers.
245: This article fixes the reach of laws. Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India. A State Legislature may make laws for the whole or any part of its State. A Parliament law may also apply outside India, if the law so provides. Each lawmaking body stays within its own territory unless the Constitution says more.
246: This article divides the power to make laws. Parliament has exclusive power over the Union List in the Seventh Schedule. The State Legislatures have exclusive power over the State List. Both may make laws over the Concurrent List. In a clash on the Concurrent List, the Parliament law prevails under article 254. The three lists are the backbone of the federal division of powers.
247: This article lets Parliament create extra courts. Parliament may by law provide for additional courts for the better administration of laws it makes. This supports the enforcement of Union laws inside the States. The courts so created serve the Union's own legislative domain.
248: This article gives Parliament the residuary power. Any matter not listed in the Concurrent List or the State List belongs to Parliament. New subjects that the framers could not foresee fall here. Subject to article 246A on GST, this power is exclusive to Parliament. It keeps the lists from leaving gaps.
249: This article lets Parliament enter the State List in the national interest. The Council of States must first pass a resolution by two thirds of its members present and voting. The resolution says that the national interest needs Parliament's lawmaking on a State List matter. The power then lasts one year at a time. Laws made under it operate like ordinary Parliament laws, and article 251 governs clashes.
250: This article covers legislation during an Emergency. While a Proclamation of Emergency is in operation, Parliament may make laws for any part of India on any State List matter. This is the widest form of the Union's legislative reach. When the Emergency ends, the laws made under it survive for six months more, unless extended by the State's consent.
251: This article settles clashes between a State law and a Parliament law made under articles 249 or 250. The State keeps the power to make its law. But if the two clash, the Parliament law prevails for the time it applies. The State law revives when the Parliament law stops. It keeps the priority rule of article 254 at work in these special cases.
252: This article lets Parliament legislate for two or more States by consent. If the legislatures of two or more States resolve that a matter on their list should be handled by Parliament, Parliament may make that law.
