A State that adopted the law may later repeal its adoption by resolution. Other States may adopt the law later. Consent converts a State subject into a shared one for that law.
253: This article gives Parliament the power to implement international agreements. Any law for giving effect to an agreement, convention, or treaty falls within this power. It applies to the whole of India. The power stands despite anything else in the Chapter. Treaties are implemented domestically by Parliament through this article.
254: This article is the clash rule between Union and State laws. If a State law is repugnant to a Parliament law on a Concurrent subject, the Parliament law prevails. The State law is void to the extent of the clash. There is one exception. If the State law was reserved for the President and received his assent, it prevails. Even then, Parliament may later pass a law to override it.
255: This article saves laws from procedural defects. No Act is invalid merely because a required recommendation or sanction was not given. The requirement must be about procedure only. This article keeps formality from destroying substance once the law is passed.
256: This article states the States' basic duty in the federal scheme. The executive power of every State is exercised to ensure compliance with Parliament's laws and existing laws in force. This is the enforcement side of the division of powers. A State does not just obey Union law; it administers it within its territory.
257: This article lets the Union direct the States. The executive power of every State must not impede the Union's executive power. The Union may give States directions it deems necessary for that purpose. Directions cover the construction of railways and national highways of Union importance. The costs of such directions are borne as agreed. Persistent default permits the President to treat it as a constitutional breakdown under article 356.
258: This article lets the Union entrust functions to States. The President may, with the consent of a State Government, entrust to that State functions the Union can exercise. This covers matters where the Union's executive power runs through the States' machinery. Consent of the State is the key. The Union may also confer powers and impose duties on a State for those functions.
259: This article no longer exists. It had provided for the armed forces in States of Part B of the First Schedule. That classification of States ended with the reorganisation of 1956. The 7th Amendment omitted the article in that year. The article has had no work to do since.
260: This article covers the Union’s role outside India. The Government of India may by agreement with another territory take on functions for it. These cover the executive, the legislature, and the courts. The agreement must follow any Indian law on foreign jurisdiction. This is how India performs agreed tasks for a neighbour.
261: This article binds the Union and the States together in law. Full faith and credit are given throughout India to public acts, records, and judicial proceedings of the Union and every State. The form of proof and the effect of such acts are as Parliament provides by law. A court decree in one State is honoured in another.
262: This article covers inter-State river water disputes. Parliament may by law provide for the adjudication of disputes over the use, distribution, or control of inter-State river waters. Parliament may also exclude such disputes from the Supreme Court and other courts. Water tribunals set up under such laws handle these disputes.
263: This article provides for an Inter-State Council. The President may establish it if the public interest so requires. The Council inquires into and advises on inter-State disputes. It investigates subjects of common interest between the Union and the States. The President defines its organisation and procedure. It is the standing forum for federal coordination.
264: This article is a reading rule for Part XII. Finance Commission means the Commission set up under article 280. Net proceeds are defined for the taxation articles that follow. The definitions keep the finance chapter steady in its terms. One meaning serves the whole Part.
265: This article is the first principle of tax law. No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law. One line carries the whole rule. Neither the Union nor a State may take money as tax without a law behind it.
266: This article creates the public funds. India and every State have a Consolidated Fund. All revenues received and loans raised go into it, and all expenditure is made from it under appropriation. There is also a public account for other moneys, which flows by the Constitution or law. No money leaves the Consolidated Fund except under article 114 or a State's equivalent.
267: This article creates the contingency funds. Parliament may establish a Contingency Fund of India. Each State may establish its own. The fund is held by the Finance Secretary or an officer, to meet unforeseen expenditure. Money spent from it must later be authorised by law through the regular budget process. It is the cushion for emergencies in public spending.
268: This article covers stamp duties. Stamp duties in the Union List are levied by the Government of India. They are collected by the States when the dutiable instrument is executed there. The proceeds belong to the States. This is a Union levy whose fruit goes to the States.
269: This article covers taxes assigned to the States. Taxes on the sale or purchase of goods, and on consignment of goods, are levied and collected by the Government of India. The net proceeds are assigned to the States and do not form part of the Consolidated Fund of India. Interstate supply is excepted, being governed by article 269A.
270: This article covers the shared taxes. Duties and taxes in the Union List, other than those of articles 268, 269, and 269A, are levied and collected by the Union. They are distributed between the Union and the States in the manner Parliament provides, on the recommendations of the Finance Commission.
271: This article lets Parliament add a surcharge. Parliament may increase any duty or tax of articles 269 and 270 by a surcharge for Union purposes. The surcharge goes to the Union. This is the Union's own margin on the shared field.
272: This article no longer exists. It had covered Union taxes that could be shared with the States by law. The 80th Amendment omitted it in 2000 as the tax sharing scheme was recast. Article 270 carries the present arrangement. The change simplified the finance chapter.
273: This article provides grants to jute growing States. Grants in lieu of the export duty on jute and jute products are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India each year. Assam, Bihar, Odisha, and West Bengal receive them. The payments run until Parliament provides otherwise.
274: This article guards the States' tax interests at the Bill stage. No Bill or amendment imposing or varying a tax in which States are interested may be introduced except on the President's recommendation. The same applies where the meaning of agricultural income or the sharing of duties changes, or a State's Consolidated Fund is charged. The President acts on a resolution of the GST Council where that article applies.
275: This article provides statutory grants to States. Parliament may by law provide sums charged on the Consolidated Fund of India as grants-in-aid of the revenues of States in need of assistance. Different sums may be fixed for different States. The article also names grants for scheduled areas and for the welfare of Scheduled Tribes, and for theadministration of scheduled areas. An expert committee's recommendations guide the tribal welfare grants.
276: This article permits a tax on professions. A State or municipality may tax professions, trades, callings, and employments. The tax cannot exceed two thousand five hundred rupees per person per year. The cap applies to the whole amount, not each law separately.
277: This article saves existing taxes. Taxes lawfully levied at the commencement of the Constitution continue. This holds even though the subject falls under a different list. The levy is treated as valid under the new order. Old taxes kept flowing without a gap.
278: This article no longer exists. It had covered agreements with the Part B States of the First Schedule on taxation. That classification of States ended with the reorganisation of 1956. The 7th Amendment omitted the article in that year. Nothing in the present scheme depends on it.
279: This article defines net proceeds. Net proceeds of a tax or duty mean the proceeds minus the cost of collection. The certificate of the Comptroller and Auditor-General is final on that amount. This keeps the sharing calculations honest and audited.
280: This article creates the Finance Commission. The President constitutes it every fifth year or sooner if needed. It recommends the distribution of net tax proceeds between the Union and the States, grants-in-aid to States, and measures to augment State funds for panchayats and municipalities. Parliament may by law add matters to its remit.
281: This article makes the Finance Commission public. The President causes every recommendation of the Commission to be laid before Parliament. An explanatory memorandum of the action taken accompanies it. The report is not filed away. It reaches the House and the record.
282: This article permits purpose grants. The Union or a State may make grants for any public purpose. The purpose need not fall within its own lawmaking domain. This is the widest spending power. It covers discretionary grants beyond the Finance Commission's formula.
283: This article covers custody of the public funds. The custody of the Consolidated and Contingency Funds, the payment of money into them, and the withdrawal from them are regulated by Parliament or the State Legislature. The same applies to moneys held outside the funds. No withdrawal without appropriation.
284: This article covers other public moneys. Deposits held by officers and courts, and moneys received for specific purposes, are paid into the public account. Their custody and use follow the rules the legislature makes. These sums are not part of the Consolidated Fund.
285: This article exempts Union property from State taxes. The property of the Union is exempt from all State or local authority taxes. Parliament may by law remove the exemption for particular cases. Where a State law taxes Union property used for trade, Parliament can override the exemption by law.
286: This article restrains State sales taxes on interstate supply. No State law may tax a supply where it takes place outside the State. It may not tax imports into the State. Parliament may set principles defining when a supply is interstate. State GST on interstate supply is void under this article.
287: This article restricts taxes on electricity. A State may not tax the consumption or sale of electricity stored, generated, or consumed by the Union or its railways. It may tax electricity consumed by the Union in manufacturing or trade if Parliament permits.
288: This article restricts State taxes on water and electricity. A State may not tax the entry of goods into a local area for Union use. It may not tax the production or supply of water or electricity by Union facilities. The President may modify these bars by order.
289: This article exempts State property from Union taxes. The property and income of a State are exempt from Union taxation. Trade or business of the State is not exempt if Parliament so provides by law. The Union cannot tax a State as it would tax a citizen.
290: This article handles shared costs and pensions. Where a court, commission, or pension spans States, the President may order how the cost is apportioned. The charge falls where the Constitution or agreement places it. This settles the sharing of such expenses.
291: This article no longer exists. It had guaranteed the privy purse payments to the former rulers of princely States. The 26th Amendment omitted it in 1971 and abolished the privileges. The recognition of rulers as such also ended. This was a founding change of the era.
292: This article permits Union borrowing. The Union may borrow on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India. Parliament sets the limits by law. The Union may also give guarantees within those limits. Borrowing is a Union executive power. Guarantees count against the same limits.
293: This article permits State borrowing. A State may borrow within India on the security of its Consolidated Fund. Its legislature sets the limits. A State may not borrow without the Union's consent if it owes the Union. The Union may lend to States or guarantee State loans.
294: This article passes the old to the new. On commencement of the Constitution, property and assets of the old Dominion vested in the Union. Rights and obligations also passed at the same moment. What belonged to a Province vested in the corresponding State. The new order inherited the old estate.
295: This article continues other succession. Property vested in an Indian State before commencement passed to the new State under the Constitution. Where there is no successor, it vests in the Union. Obligations follow the property into the same hands. Nothing falls between two stools.
296: This article covers property without an owner. Property that would have passed to the British Crown by escheat or lapse now vests in the State, or the Union if no State applies. Bona vacantia within a State goes the same way. Ownerless property finds a public home.
297: This article vests the offshore wealth. Lands, minerals, and things of value under the ocean vest in the Union. The cover extends to the territorial waters, the shelf, and the zone. The Union uses them for the common good of the country.
298: This article lets the governments do business. The Union and each State may carry on any trade or business. They may acquire and hold property for the purpose. The power serves public ends chosen by the government. It stands beside the ordinary market participants in the field.
299: This article sets the form of government contracts. Contracts are made in the name of the President or Governor. They must be expressed and executed on the authority of the officer authorised. No contract fails for want of form. No person can sue on a contract not made in this manner.
300: This article names the governments in court. The Government of India sues and is sued as the Union of India. A State government sues and is sued in the State's name. The old dominion liability continues in the new public hands.
301: This article declares the economic union of India. Trade, commerce, and intercourse throughout the territory of India shall be free. This is the general rule of the national market. The articles that follow carry the restrictions. The clause anchors one market across all the States.
302: This article lets Parliament restrict the freedom where needed. Parliament may by law impose restrictions on trade between States in the public interest. The interest must be stated in the law. Restrictions by Parliament are the exception that keeps the union honest.
303: This article is the anti discrimination rule of the economic union. Neither Parliament nor a State may favour one State over another in trade law. One narrow exception exists. Parliament may act for a State in scarcity. Even then, a surplus State cannot be discriminated against in distribution.
304: This article lets a State limit trade in its own way. A State may impose reasonable taxes on goods imported from other States in the same manner as local goods. A State may also restrict trade in the public interest, but such a Bill needs the President's previous sanction. The sanction is the Union's check.
305: This article saves laws that came before. Existing laws are not affected by articles 301 and 303. Laws providing for State monopolies are also saved. The President may by order bring such laws under review and modify them. The national market works with the old charters.
306: This article no longer exists. It had given certain Part B States special powers over trade. That classification of States ended with the reorganisation of 1956. The 7th Amendment omitted the article in that year. The general trade chapter now covers every State alike.
307: This article provides the referee of the trade chapter. Parliament may by law appoint an authority for carrying out articles 301 to 304. The authority may also carry out any other trade provisions Parliament assigns. A named forum settles the frictions of the common market.
308: This article is a reading rule for Part XIV on the services. The printed text excludes the State of Jammu and Kashmir from the expression State in this Part of the Constitution. The exclusion belongs to that State’s old special constitutional position. The chapters on services read with this lens in mind.
309: This article lets each legislature set its own service rules. The appropriate legislature may regulate recruitment and conditions of service of persons serving the Union or a State. This covers civil and criminal posts. A law may delegate rulemaking to the President or Governor. The services are run under this authority.
310: This article fixes the tenure of public servants. A member of a defence or civil service holds office during the pleasure of the President or Governor. The pleasure doctrine is the rule. A civil servant may be dismissed only under article 311 safeguards.
311: This article protects civil servants in disciplinary matters. No dismissal or reduction in rank without an inquiry and a chance to answer. The second protection bars a second inquiry on the same facts after one has been made. The safeguards make the pleasure doctrine honest.
312: This article creates the all India services. The Council of States must first resolve by two thirds of members present and voting that the national interest needs a new common service. Parliament then creates it. The IAS, IPS, and IFoS are the present services under this article. Recruitment is by a Union exam, posting covers the States.
313: This article is a bridge from the old services. Until other provision is made, laws in force before commencement continue to apply to the new services. The old rules carry into the new order. The bridge ends when the new law is made.
314: This article no longer exists. It had protected existing officers of certain former Indian State services. The protection ran until their integration was complete. The 28th Amendment omitted the article in 1972. The services now run under the ordinary provisions.
315: This article provides the Public Service Commissions. There is one for the Union and one for each State. Two or more States may agree to a Joint Commission. A State legislature may provide a Joint Commission for its own public services. The UPSC and State PSCs are the recruitment gatekeepers of the services.
316: This article covers the appointment of Commission members. The Chairman and members of the Union Commission are appointed by the President. For State Commissions, the Governor appoints. Half the members have held office for at least ten years under a government. A member holds office for six years or until sixty two in the Union, sixty two in the States, whichever comes first.
317: This article protects Commission members. The Chairman or a member may be removed only by the President on grounds of misbehaviour after a Supreme Court inquiry on a reference. Insolvency or paid outside employment also ends the office. The Governor may suspend a member pending the reference. This is the same shield that High Court judges carry.
318: This article lets the President or Governor set the conditions of service of Commission members. The regulations cover conditions of service that the Constitution does not fix. The President or Governor makes them by regulation. It completes the working framework of the Commissions.
319: This article bars Commission members from future office. On ceasing to hold office, the Chairman of the Union Commission is ineligible for further government employment. A member of the UPSC is eligible only to be Chairman of the UPSC or a State Commission. A State Commission member may only go to another State Commission chair. The bar keeps the Commissions neutral.
320: This article sets the functions of the Commissions. They conduct examinations for appointments to the services. They are consulted on all recruitment matters. They advise on disciplinary matters and on claims for pensions. The consultation is the heart of the role.
321: This article extends the work of the Commissions. The appropriate legislature may confer additional functions on a Commission. The extension may cover any service matter the law chooses. The Commissions grow by statute. Their core duty of recruitment stays the same.
322: This article charges the Commission expenses on the public funds. The expenses of a Commission, including salaries and pensions, are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the Union or the State. The charge protects the Commissions from the annual vote. Their independence is funded by the Constitution.
323: This article brings the Commissions under review. The Union Commission presents an annual report to the President. A State Commission reports to the Governor. The report must be laid before the legislature with a memorandum of the cases where advice was not accepted. The record keeps the Commissions accountable.
324: This article vests the election machinery in the Election Commission. The conduct of elections to Parliament, to the State Legislatures, and to the offices of President and Vice President rests with it. The Chief Election Commissioner has the removal shield of a Supreme Court Judge. Regional Commissioners assist the body. The Commission is the referee of Indian elections.
325: This article builds one common citizenship into the electoral roll. There is one general electoral roll for every constituency. No person is ineligible for it by reason of religion, race, caste, or sex. The roll is one for the whole people of the constituency.
326: This article gives the vote to every adult. Elections to the House of the People and to every State Assembly are on the basis of adult suffrage. A person qualified is one who is a citizen and is not less than eighteen years on the qualifying date. One person, one vote, one value.
327: This article lets Parliament legislate on elections. Parliament may by law make provision on all matters relating to elections to the Union and State legislatures. The law covers delimitation, rolls, and the mechanics of the vote. The Representation of the People Acts stand on this article.
328: This article lets a State legislate where Parliament has not. A State Legislature may make provision on elections to its own legislature so far as Parliament has not covered the field. The Union law prevails where both exist. The State fills the gaps.
329: This article keeps courts out of election mechanics. The validity of delimitation laws cannot be questioned in court. An election cannot be called in question except by an election petition to the authority the legislature provides. The disputes go to the process the law builds.
330: This article reserves seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in the Lok Sabha. The reserved seats are in proportion to their population as nearly as possible. The Scheduled Tribes of the autonomous districts of Assam have their own arrangement. Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Nagaland have no reservation where tribal seats are already the whole.
331: This article lets the President nominate Anglo Indians to the Lok Sabha. Where the community is not adequately represented, the President may nominate not more than two members. The 104th Amendment ended this nomination in 2020. The printed article remains with the mechanism it carried.
332: This article reserves seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in State Assemblies. The reservation follows population proportion in the State. The Scheduled Tribes of Assam’s autonomous districts have their own arrangement. The pattern follows article 330 at the State level of the system.
333: This article let Governors nominate an Anglo Indian to a State Assembly. Where the community needed representation, the Governor could nominate one member. The 104th Amendment ended the nomination in 2020. The printed article remains without live work. It stands as part of the record.
334: This article fixes the horizon of the reservations. The reservation of seats and special representation were to cease after a set period, subject to extension by amendment. The Anglo Indian representation was abolished by the 104th Amendment in 2020. The printed date now reads 2030 for the scheduled caste and tribe reservations. Each extension has been made by amendment.
335: This article balances reservation with efficiency in the services. The claims of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes are weighed against the efficiency of administration. The 82nd Amendment added that relaxed marks do not bar promotion. The bridge between social justice and administration is drawn here.
336: This article was a transitional provision for the Anglo Indian community in services. It covered appointments for the first two years after commencement. Those years closed long ago. It has no present work at all. The printed article remains as history.
337: This article was a transitional provision for educational grants to the Anglo Indian community. It covered the first three financial years after commencement. Those years closed long ago as well. It has no present application. The printed article remains as history.
338: This article creates the National Commission for Scheduled Castes. It investigates and safeguards their rights and safeguards under the Constitution. It inquires into complaints of deprivation. It participates in planning for their development. The Commission reports to the President, who lays the report before Parliament.
339: This article gives the Union a hand in the scheduled areas. The President may appoint a Commission to report on the administration of Scheduled Areas and the welfare of Scheduled Tribes. The report is laid before each House of Parliament. The Union keeps the oversight of these areas.
340: This article lets the President appoint a backward classes commission. The Commission investigates the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes. It reports on the steps needed for their improvement. The report goes to the President and then to Parliament. The Mandal Commission was appointed under this article.
341: This article defines the Scheduled Castes. The President may by public notification specify the castes, races, or tribes deemed Scheduled Castes in a State or Union territory, after consulting the Governor. Parliament may by law include or exclude any caste. The notified list is the operative one.
342: This article defines the Scheduled Tribes. The President may notify the tribes deemed Scheduled Tribes for each State or Union territory. Parliament may include or exclude any tribe by law. The same pattern as article 341, for the tribes. The notified list is the operative one.
343: This article makes Hindi in Devanagari script the official language of the Union. The form of numerals for official purposes is the international form. English continues for official purposes during the transition, and Parliament extended its use by law. Hindi is the official language, not the national language of India.
344: This article provides a language review body. The President appoints a Commission on official language every five years at first, and later every ten. Parliament also forms a Committee of thirty members to look at the report. The scheme keeps the progress of Hindi under review.
345: This article lets States choose their official language or languages. A State may adopt one or more languages in use in the State or Hindi. The choice is subject to the Union link language scheme of articles 346 and 347.
346: This article fixes the language between two States. The official language of the Union is the language for communication between one State and another, and between a State and the Union. Where two States agree, they may use another language. The Union language is the channel.
347: This article lets the President recognise a State language. If a substantial proportion of a State's population demands it, the President may direct that the language be recognised throughout the State or any part. The demand of a linguistic group finds a constitutional answer.
348: This article keeps English in the courts. All proceedings in the Supreme Court and High Courts are in English until Parliament provides otherwise. Parliament may allow Hindi or other languages in High Court judgments with the Governor's consent and the President's previous sanction. The language of the record stays protected.
349: This article was a transitional brake on language laws. For fifteen years after commencement, no Bill restricting language rights could be introduced except on the President's recommendation after a Commission's consideration. The period ended in 1965. The safeguard is now spent.
350: This article protects the citizen's grievance language. Any person may submit a representation for redress of grievances to any Union or State authority in any language used in the Union or the State. The right belongs to every person, not only citizens.
351: This article directs the development of Hindi. The Union is to promote the spread of Hindi and develop it as a medium of expression for the composite culture of India. The sources are Hindustani and the languages listed in the Eighth Schedule. The directive guides without displacing other languages.
352: This article provides the national Emergency. The President proclaims it when the security of India or any part is threatened. The grounds are war, external attack, or armed rebellion. The 44th Amendment put internal disturbance out of the list and required written Cabinet advice. Approval must come within a month, and the run is six months at a time.
353: This article states the effect of an Emergency. The Union's executive power extends to directions to States on anything. Parliament gains power to legislate on State subjects. The Lok Sabha's term and State Assemblies may be extended a year at a time. The federal structure tilts to the Union while the Emergency runs.
354: This article lets revenue sharing bend during an Emergency. The President may by order suspend the ordinary distribution provisions of articles 268 to 279. All taxes then go into the single distributable pool. The finance scheme yields to the emergency.
355: This article states the Union’s protective duty. The Union protects every State against attack from outside and disturbance within. It also ensures that every State government runs by the Constitution. This duty backs the Emergency and the President’s rule provisions of this Part.
356: This article provides President's rule. If the President is satisfied that a State's government cannot be carried on by the Constitution, the President may assume the State's executive functions. The State legislature's powers pass to Parliament. The proclamation needs approval within two months and runs six months at a time, with limits on the total span.
357: This article covers lawmaking during President's rule. Parliament may exercise the State legislature's powers. The President may authorise the State Governor to make laws when Parliament is not in session. Laws made survive the President's rule unless repealed by the State.
358: This article once suspended all of article 19 in a war emergency. The 44th Amendment narrowed it to armed rebellion or war. Even then, only the freedoms relevant to the emergency fall. The six freedoms revive when the emergency ends. The rights are no longer switched off wholesale.
359: This article lets the President suspend the right to move courts for fundamental rights during an Emergency. The declaration names the rights. Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended after the 44th Amendment. The suspension ends when the Emergency ends. Emergency does not touch life and personal liberty.
360: This article provides the financial emergency. If the money stability or credit of India is threatened, the President may proclaim it. Directions may issue to States on money matters, including pay cuts. Approval must come within two months. The emergency runs until revoked. It has never been used.
361: This article protects the President and Governors from court process. They are not answerable to any court for official acts. No criminal case may start against the President or a Governor while in office. Civil arrest proceedings need two months' notice. The shield covers the office, not personal acts before assuming it.
362: This article no longer exists. It had kept the rights and privileges of the rulers of the Indian States. The 26th Amendment abolished the privileges in 1971 and omitted the article. The princely order ended with the same amendment. Nothing depends on it now.
363: This article bars courts from disputes under certain agreements. The Supreme Court and other courts cannot question treaties, agreements, or covenants excluded by the President's notification. The bar is subject to article 143. The listed pacts are taken out of the courts.
364: This article brings major ports and aerodromes under Union control. The President may by notification vest in the Union the property and functions of major ports and aerodromes. Parliament makes the consequential law. The Union keeps the great transport gateways.
365: This article turns disobedience into a constitutional breakdown. Where a State fails to comply with Union directions, the failure may be treated as a failure of the constitutional machinery. President's rule under article 356 may follow. The sanction behind Union directions is here.
366: This article is the Constitution's own glossary. It defines the key expressions: State, law, State law, India, and the many special terms of the Constitution. The definitions bind the reading of every other article. It is the dictionary the courts use first.
367: This article supplies the reading rules. The General Clauses Act, 1897 applies to the Constitution with adaptations. References to the Government of India Act are to be read with the adaptations and orders. Expressions of the old Act carry their old meaning. The bridge from the old constitutional law is drawn here.
368: This article gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution. An amendment starts as a Bill in either House. Each House must pass it by a majority of its total membership and by two thirds of the members present and voting. The President then gives assent. Some amendments also need ratification by half the state legislatures. Courts have held that this power cannot destroy the basic structure of the Constitution.
370: This article contained the temporary provisions for the State of Jammu and Kashmir. It limited Parliament's power to legislate for the State to matters in the Instrument of Accession, with the State's concurrence for more. It left the State its own constitution and flag. In 2019, Presidential Orders applied the Constitution to the territory and it was reorganised into Union territories. The printed text remains in the official edition.
371: This article gives the Governor of Maharashtra and Gujarat a special responsibility. The President may by order provide for the constitution of separate development boards for different regions. For Maharashtra, the regions are Vidarbha, Marathwada, and the rest of the State. For Gujarat, they are Saurashtra and Kutch. The boards report on the balanced development of their regions.
21A: This article makes free and compulsory education a right for every child aged six to fourteen. The State must provide this education. A child can claim it as a matter of right, not charity. It was added in 2002 so that schooling becomes a duty of the State.
31A: This article saves certain laws from being struck down for violating fundamental rights. It covers laws about acquiring estates and similar property reforms. Land reform laws cannot be attacked merely for limiting property rights. Courts later read this saving as subject to the basic structure of the Constitution.
31B: This article protects laws placed in the Ninth Schedule from challenge under fundamental rights. Laws added to that schedule are shielded even if they conflict with Part III. In 2007 the Supreme Court held that laws added after 1973 can still be tested against the basic structure of the Constitution.
31C: This article shields laws that carry out certain directive principles. Those principles deal with sharing resources and reducing wealth gaps. Such laws cannot be struck down under Articles 14 and 19. Since 1973, the shield does not cover laws that damage the basic structure of the Constitution.
31D: This article was inserted by the Forty second Amendment to save laws against anti national activities. It never came into effect. It was omitted by the Constitution Forty third Amendment Act in 1977. The Constitution today contains no such article.
32A: This article was inserted by the Forty second Amendment and omitted by the Forty third Amendment in 1977. It had removed the power of courts to examine State laws in certain proceedings under Article 32. It never took effect and no longer exists.
39A: This article asks the State to make justice equal in practice. The legal system should promote justice on the basis of equal opportunity. The State must provide free legal aid, by law, by schemes, or in any other way. The goal is that no citizen is denied justice for want of money or other disability. The 42nd Amendment inserted this article in 1976.
43A: This article asks the State to bring workers into management. By law or other means, the State should secure the participation of workers in running undertakings or establishments engaged in any industry. The 42nd Amendment inserted this article in 1976. The idea is a voice for workers in decisions that shape their work.
43B: This article asks the State to promote cooperative societies. The State should foster their voluntary formation, autonomous working, democratic control, and professional management. The 97th Amendment inserted this article in 2012. A cooperative is a body owned and run by its members. The principle supports them without putting them under state control.
48A: This article asks the State to protect and improve the environment. It also covers forests and wildlife, which the State must safeguard for the country. The 42nd Amendment inserted this article in 1976. Courts often read it with Article 21 in cases about pollution and forests.
51A: This article lists the duties of every citizen. Respect the Constitution, the national flag, and the anthem. Cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle. Protect the unity of India and its environment. Develop scientific temper and humanism. Protect public property and strive for excellence. Courts cannot punish a breach directly, but laws may be read in its light.
124A: This article creates the National Judicial Appointments Commission. The 99th Amendment inserted it in 2014 to recommend judges for the Supreme Court and the High Courts. The Supreme Court struck it down in 2015 as unconstitutional. The text remains printed in the official edition, but the Commission never took effect. The collegium of judges continues to make the recommendations.
124B: This article lists the functions of the National Judicial Appointments Commission. It was to recommend persons for appointment as Chief Justice of India and Judges of the Supreme Court. It was also to recommend Chief Justices and Judges of the High Courts, and their transfers. The Commission was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015 before it could work.
124C: This article would have let Parliament regulate the appointment procedure for judges by law. It belongs to the National Judicial Appointments Commission scheme of the 99th Amendment. The Supreme Court struck that scheme down in 2015. No such law has been made.
131A: This article no longer exists. It had given the Supreme Court exclusive jurisdiction over questions about the constitutional validity of Central laws. The 43rd Amendment omitted it in 1978. High Courts regained their ordinary jurisdiction in such matters. The omission restored the position that existed before the 42nd Amendment made the change.
134A: This article creates the certificate for appeal. A High Court may grant it on its own motion, and a party may also apply for it. The certificate is what articles 132, 133, and 134 require. It opens the door to the Supreme Court.
139A: This article lets the Supreme Court unify cases. Where the same question of law is pending before the Supreme Court and one or more High Courts, the cases may be transferred and heard together. The Court may act on its own motion or on an application. It may also transfer a case from one High Court to another for the ends of justice.
144A: This article no longer exists. It had required a special bench when the Court decided questions about the constitutional validity of Central or State laws. The 43rd Amendment omitted it in 1978. The ordinary bench arrangements now govern such cases.
228A: This article no longer exists. It had set special rules for State High Courts deciding questions about the constitutional validity of State laws. The 43rd Amendment omitted it in 1978. The ordinary jurisdiction of the High Courts was restored after that. The omission returned such cases to the ordinary bench.
239A: This article lets Parliament create legislatures for Union territories. Parliament may by law create a legislature for Puducherry, elected or partly nominated. It may also create a Council of Ministers for the territory. Such a law is not treated as an amendment of the Constitution under article 368. Puducherry today has an elected Assembly under this article.
239AA: This article gives Delhi its special constitutional scheme. The National Capital Territory has a Legislative Assembly chosen by direct election. It can make laws on the State List and the Concurrent List, except public order, police, and land. It has a Council of Ministers of not more than ten per cent of the Assembly's strength, collectively responsible to the Assembly. Parliament's law prevails where its own laws collide with the Assembly's.
239AB: This article covers a breakdown in Delhi’s government. The President must first be satisfied that the administration cannot be carried on under article 239AA. The President may then suspend its provisions by order. The Assembly is suspended. The President assumes its powers for the period. This is the President’s rule provision for Delhi.
239B: This article gives administrators the ordinance power. When the legislature of a territory such as Puducherry is not meeting, the administrator may issue Ordinances. The gap is treated like the recess of a State Legislature under article 213. An Ordinance issued on the President’s instructions counts as an Act of the legislature. Anything beyond its power is void.
243A: This article recognises the Gram Sabha. A Gram Sabha may exercise such powers and perform such functions at the village level as the Legislature of a State provides by law. The Gram Sabha is the general body of village voters. It is the base of the whole panchayat structure.
243B: This article requires Panchayats at three levels in every State. There shall be Panchayats at the village, intermediate, and district levels. A State with a population not exceeding twenty lakhs may skip the intermediate level. Every State therefore has an elected rural local government structure under this Part.
243C: This article sets the composition of Panchayats. All seats are filled by direct election from the constituencies of the Panchayat area. The chairpersons of village Panchayats may sit in the intermediate Panchayat. The chairpersons of intermediate Panchayats may sit in the district one. The chairperson at the village level is chosen as the State law provides. Seats are spread so that each covers a similar population.
243D: This article provides for reservation of seats in Panchayats. Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population. Not less than one third of the seats are reserved for women, including the women of those groups. The State may reserve seats for backward classes. Offices of chairpersons are reserved in the same manner as the State law provides.
243E: This article fixes the term of a Panchayat at five years. If dissolved earlier, a Panchayat does not live beyond its original term. An election must be completed before the term expires. If the Panchayat is dissolved, the election must be held within six months. The reconstituted Panchayat serves only the remainder of the original term. No law amendment can force an early dissolution.
243F: This article lists the disqualifications for Panchayat membership. A person must be qualified to be a State Legislature member and must not be disqualified by any law. A person over twenty one years cannot be disqualified for being below the minimum age for the State Legislature. Questions of disqualification are decided as the State law provides.
243G: This article gives Panchayats their purpose. A State may by law endow Panchayats with the powers and authority needed to work as institutions of self-government. The law may provide for planning and implementation of schemes for economic development and social justice. The twenty nine subjects of the Eleventh Schedule are the domain of this power. Village plans may feed into district plans.
243H: This article gives Panchayats their money powers. A State may authorise a Panchayat to levy, collect, and appropriate taxes, duties, tolls, and fees. A State may also assign to a Panchayat taxes collected by the State. And a State may make grants-in-aid to Panchayats from its Consolidated Fund. A State may establish a Fund for each Panchayat and its use.
243I: This article requires a State Finance Commission for Panchayats. The Governor constitutes a Finance Commission within one year of the 73rd Amendment and every five years after. The Commission reviews the financial position of the Panchayats. It recommends the sharing of State taxes, grants, and improvements to the Panchayats' own revenue. The Governor places the report before the State Legislature.
243J: This article covers Panchayat accounts. A State may by law provide for the keeping of accounts by Panchayats. It may provide for the audit of those accounts. The Comptroller and Auditor-General may be entrusted with the audit. Accountability flows through the State’s own arrangement.
243K: This article places Panchayat elections with an independent commission. The superintendence, direction, and control of Panchayat elections vest in a State Election Commission. It consists of a State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor. The Commissioner can be removed only as a High Court Judge is removed. The Governor provides staff when the Commission asks.
243L: This article extends Part IX to Union territories. The panchayat rules apply to the territories as they apply to States. Where the text says Governor, it reads administrator. Where it says State Legislature, it reads the legislature of the territory. The President may direct further changes by order.
243M: This article exempts certain areas from Part IX. The whole Part does not apply to Scheduled Areas and tribal areas under article 244. It does not apply to Nagaland, Meghalaya, and Mizoram. It does not apply to the hill areas of Manipur with District Councils. District level Panchayats do not apply to the Darjeeling hill areas. Parliament may extend the Part to these areas by law with exceptions.
243N: This article saves existing Panchayat laws. Laws in force before the 73rd Amendment continue until amended or repealed. Panchayats already functioning continue until their term expires. The saving runs for one year from the amendment, extendable by law. States then had to align their law with the new Part.
243O: This article keeps courts out of Panchayat election mechanics. The validity of laws on delimitation and seat allotment cannot be questioned in court. An election to a Panchayat cannot be called in question except through an election petition to the authority the State law provides. Election disputes stay inside the process the law builds.
243P: This article defines the words of Part IXA. A Committee is one constituted under article 243S for wards. A district means a district of a State. A Metropolitan area means an area with a population of ten lakhs or more, covering one or more districts. A Municipal area means the territorial area of a Municipality. A Municipality is an institution of self-government for an urban area. A Panchayat is defined in Part IX.
243Q: This article requires Municipalities in every State. A Nagar Panchayat is constituted for a transitional area. A Municipal Council for a smaller urban area. A Municipal Corporation for a larger urban area. The Governor notifies what is transitional, smaller urban, or larger urban. A State may by law constitute other urban local bodies with powers, but this Part governs the three main types.
243R: This article sets the composition of Municipalities. All seats are filled by direct election from the constituencies of the Municipal area. The State may provide for seats for chairpersons of Committees. MPs and MLAs from the area may also sit in the Municipality. They do not vote there unless they are elected members.
243S: This article provides for Wards Committees. A Municipality with a population of three lakhs or more is divided into wards, and Wards Committees are constituted for them. Each Committee has members of the Municipality elected from the wards. The State Legislature may make provision for the composition and powers of these Committees. One or more wards may form a Committee.
243T: This article provides for reservation of seats in Municipalities. Seats are reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population. Not less than one third of the seats are reserved for women, including the women of those groups. The State may reserve seats for backward classes. Offices of chairpersons are reserved in the same manner as the State law provides.
243U: This article fixes the term of a Municipality at five years. If dissolved earlier, it does not live beyond its original term. An election must be completed before the term expires. If the Municipality is dissolved, the election must be held within six months. The reconstituted body serves only the remainder of the original term. A no-confidence motion cannot shorten the term in the last six months.
243V: This article lists the disqualifications for Municipality membership. A person must be qualified to be a State Legislature member. The person must not be disqualified by any law. A person over twenty one years cannot be barred for being below the age for the State Legislature. Questions of disqualification are decided as the State law provides.
243W: This article gives Municipalities their purpose. A State may by law endow Municipalities with the powers and authority needed to work as institutions of self-government. The law may provide for planning and implementation of schemes for economic development and social justice. The eighteen subjects of the Twelfth Schedule are the domain of this power. Municipalities handle the urban functions of that list.
243X: This article gives Municipalities their money powers. A State may authorise a Municipality to levy, collect, and appropriate taxes, duties, tolls, and fees. A State may also assign to a Municipality taxes collected by the State. And a State may make grants-in-aid to Municipalities from its Consolidated Fund. A State may establish a Fund for each Municipality and its use.
243Y: This article ties Municipalities into the State Finance Commission. The Commission set up under article 243I also reviews the finances of the Municipalities. It looks at both the Panchayats and the Municipalities. It recommends the sharing of State taxes and grants. It also suggests ways to improve their own revenue.
243Z: This article covers Municipality accounts. A State may by law provide for the maintenance of accounts by Municipalities. It may provide for the audit of those accounts. The Comptroller and Auditor-General may be entrusted with the audit. Accountability flows through the State's own arrangement.
243ZA: This article places Municipality elections with the State Election Commission. The conduct of Municipal elections vests in that Commission. It is the same body that runs Panchayat elections under article 243K. The Commissioner can be removed only as a High Court Judge is removed. The Governor provides staff when the Commission asks.
243ZB: This article extends Part IXA to Union territories. The Municipality rules apply to the territories as they apply to States. Where the text says Governor, it reads administrator. Where it says State Legislature, it reads the legislature of the territory. The President may direct further changes by order.
243ZC: This article exempts certain areas from Part IXA. The whole Part does not apply to the Scheduled Areas and tribal areas under article 244. Parliament may however extend the Part to a Scheduled Area by law, with exceptions and modifications it chooses.
243ZD: This article provides for District Planning Committees. Every State constitutes such a Committee at the district level. It consolidates the plans prepared by the Panchayats and the Municipalities in the district. It prepares a draft development plan for the district as a whole. Four fifths of its members are elected from among the elected members of the local bodies, in proportion to their strength.
243ZE: This article provides for Metropolitan Planning Committees. Every Metropolitan area gets such a Committee. It prepares a draft development plan for the whole Metropolitan area. At least two thirds of its members are elected from among the elected members of the Municipalities and chairpersons of the Panchayats in the area, in proportion to their strength. The Committee answers to the region, not one city.
243ZF: This article saves existing Municipality laws. Laws in force before the 74th Amendment continue until amended or repealed. Municipalities already functioning continue until their term expires. The saving runs for one year from the amendment, extendable by law. States then had to align their law with the new Part.
243ZG: This article keeps courts out of Municipality election mechanics. The validity of laws on delimitation and seat allotment cannot be questioned in court. An election to a Municipality can be challenged only by an election petition. The petition goes to the authority the State law provides. Election disputes stay inside that process.
243ZH: This article defines the words of Part IXB. A board means the board of directors of a co-operative society. A co-operative society is a society registered under a State law on co-operation. A multi-State co-operative society is registered under a Central law. An authorised person is one referred to in article 243ZQ. The Part governs the working of these societies.
243ZJ: This article covers the board of a co-operative society. The board consists of the number of directors the State Legislature provides by law. The maximum number is twenty one. The term of the board is five years from the date of election. The State may provide for the reservation of one seat for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes and two for women, by election.
243ZK: This article sets the timing of board elections. The election of a board is conducted before the expiry of its term. If a board is superseded or dissolved, the election is conducted within six months. The State Election Commission or an equivalent body superintends the election. The process cannot be left pending indefinitely.
243ZL: This article restrains supersession of a board. No board may be superseded or kept under suspension for more than six months. An administrator is appointed for the interim period. A superseded board gets a chance to present its case before the action. This keeps State control over societies within firm limits.
243ZM: This article covers the audit of co-operative societies. A State may by law provide for the maintenance of accounts by co-operative societies. It may provide for the audit of those accounts. The audit is carried out by an auditor appointed by the State Government or an equivalent authority. Accountability flows through the State's arrangement.
243ZN: This article covers general body meetings. A State may by law provide that the annual general body meeting of every society is convened within a period it fixes. The meeting is the members' own forum. It keeps the board answerable to the general body. The State sets the outer time limit.
243ZO: This article gives members a right to information. A State may by law provide for access by every member to the books, information, and accounts of the society. The member may get copies of documents in the manner the law provides. Transparency toward the member is a constitutional duty of the society.
243ZP: This article covers returns. Every co-operative society files returns within six months of the close of each financial year. The returns go to the authority the State Government designates. The State may specify the contents of the returns. Filing keeps the society's record current before the State.
243ZQ: This article covers offences and penalties. A State may by law make provisions for offences relating to co-operative societies. It may provide penalties for such offences. The law defines the authorised person for this purpose. Enforcement rests with the State's framework.
243ZR: This article applies Part IXB to multi-State co-operative societies. The provisions apply with one change. Where the text says State Legislature, it reads Parliament. Multi-State societies are set up under a Central law. They get the same guarantees as other societies. The change keeps one rule across the two kinds of law.
243ZS: This article extends Part IXB to Union territories. The provisions apply to the territories with the changes the President directs. For a territory without a legislature, the State Legislature reads as the President. The President’s order settles the rest of the details.
243ZT: This article saves existing co-operative society laws. Laws in force before the 97th Amendment continue until amended or repealed. The saving runs for one year from the amendment, extendable by law. States then had to align their law with the new Part.
244A: This article allows an autonomous State within Assam. Parliament may by law form an autonomous State comprising the tribal areas of Assam, wholly or in part. Such a law may create a local legislature and Council of Ministers for the area. It may specify the matters within their powers. The provision has never been used.
246A: This article creates a shared power over the goods and services tax. Parliament and every State Legislature may make laws on GST. Parliament has exclusive power on the interstate supply of goods and services. This shared field was inserted by the 101st Amendment in 2016. It works together with the GST Council under article 279A.
257A: This article no longer exists. It had provided for assistance to States by deployment of armed forces or other forces of the Union. It was part of the Emergency era changes of the 42nd Amendment. The 44th Amendment omitted it in 1978. The general provisions on the Union’s armed forces remain elsewhere.
258A: This article lets a State entrust functions to the Union. The Governor may, with the consent of the Government of India, entrust functions to the Union. The flow of functions can go both ways between the two levels. This article was added by the 7th Amendment in 1956.
268A: This article no longer exists. It had provided for service tax levied by the Union and collected and shared with the States. The 101st Amendment omitted it in 2016. The Goods and Services Tax replaced the whole arrangement. Article 268 next to it still governs stamp duties.
269A: This article governs GST on interstate supplies. Goods and services tax on supplies in the course of inter-State trade is levied and collected by the Government of India. The tax is apportioned between the Union and the States under a law of Parliament on the recommendations of the GST Council. The interstate component is called the integrated tax.
279A: This article creates the GST Council. The Union Finance Minister chairs it. State finance ministers are members. The Council makes recommendations on GST rates, exemptions, and the sharing of the tax. Its decisions are taken by a three fourths weighted vote, with the Union holding a third of the weight. The Council is the standing forum of the GST union.
290A: This article provides for the Devaswom Funds. A fixed annual sum is charged on the Consolidated Fund of Kerala for the Devaswom Funds of temples. A similar charge exists for Tamil Nadu. These payments support temple funds as the Constitution fixed them.
300A: This article protects property. No person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law. The 44th Amendment inserted it in 1978 after the old property right was removed from the fundamental rights. Property is now a constitutional right, not a fundamental one. Deprivation needs a law behind it.
312A: This article lets Parliament adjust all India service conditions. Parliament may vary or revoke conditions of service of all India service officers. The power covers remuneration, leave, and pension, and works both ways in time. The Rajya Sabha resolution is not needed for these adjustments.
329A: This article no longer exists. It had made special provision for elections to Parliament in the case of the Prime Minister and the Speaker. It belongs to the Emergency era. The 44th Amendment omitted it in 1978. The ordinary election law applies to all candidates alike.
330A: This article reserves seats for women in the House of the People. It was inserted by the 106th Amendment in 2023. The reservation is one third of the seats. It takes effect after the delimitation that follows the relevant census, as article 334A provides. The Essentials page of this site carries the same caveat.
332A: This article reserves seats for women in every State Legislative Assembly. It was inserted with article 330A by the 106th Amendment. The reservation is one third of the seats. It too waits for the delimitation after the relevant census. The Delhi assembly is included by reference.
334A: This article controls when the women's reservation under the 106th Amendment takes effect. The reservation covers the Lok Sabha, the state assemblies, and the Delhi assembly. It comes into effect after a delimitation done for this purpose, following the relevant census figures. Reserved seats continue till the date Parliament fixes by law. Rotation follows each later delimitation. Until then, existing representation is not disturbed.
338A: This article creates the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes. It was separated from the 89th Amendment's division of the old joint commission. It investigates matters relating to safeguards for Scheduled Tribes. It reports to the President, who lays the report before Parliament.
338B: This article creates the National Commission for Backward Classes. It was inserted by the 102nd Amendment in 2018. It examines requests for inclusion in the backward class lists. It hears complaints of over or under inclusion. The lists for each State are notified under article 342A.
342A: This article defines the socially and educationally backward classes. The President notifies the list for each State or Union territory after consulting the Governor. Parliament may include or exclude by law. Only the Parliament list prevails for the Central list. States keep their own lists under the 105th Amendment's restoration.
350A: This article asks States to teach children in their mother tongue. Every State and local authority is to provide facilities for primary instruction in the mother tongue. The right belongs to children of linguistic minority groups. The President may direct a State to secure the facilities.
350B: This article creates a Special Officer for linguistic minorities. The President appoints the officer. The officer looks into all matters on safeguards for such minorities. The officer reports to the President on them. The report is laid before Parliament each year.
359A: This article no longer exists. It had applied the emergency provisions of Part XVIII to the State of Punjab. That was during the disturbance of the late 1980s. The 63rd Amendment omitted it in 1990. The general emergency provisions now govern every State alike.
361A: This article protects the press reporting of legislatures. No civil or criminal case lies for a substantially true report of the House. The report must be without malice. Broadcast reports were later added. Honest reporting of the House is safe.
361B: This article bars disqualified members from office. A member unseated for defection cannot take a paid political post. The bar runs for the term of the disqualification, or until the House term ends, whichever is earlier. It closes the defection reward route.
363A: This article abolishes the princely order. The recognition of rulers as Princes, Chiefs, or other persons ceases. The rights and privileges of rulership are abolished. The 26th Amendment inserted it in 1971. Privy purse payments also ended with the same amendment.
371B: This article gives Assam a special provision. The President may by order provide for a committee of the State's Legislative Assembly. The committee is constituted in a way that gives representation to the tribal areas of the State. It considers and reports on matters of interest to those areas.
371D: This article gives Andhra Pradesh and Telangana their special provisions. The President may by order provide equitable opportunities in public employment and in education across the State. The order may organise posts and admissions by zones or local areas. It may also set up an Administrative Tribunal to hear service matters. The article was made for the Andhra Pradesh reorganisation and now serves both States.
371F: This article sets Sikkim's special provisions after it joined India in 1975. The Legislative Assembly of Sikkim has not less than thirty members. Sikkim keeps one seat in the Lok Sabha. Existing laws and courts continue subject to adaptation. Property rights and old customs are protected as the article provides.
